meta.blurb: At seventeen, Marco Polo leaves Venice for a court so far away that the road takes years. There he sees paper money, black stones that burn and a Great Khan who likes him. Back home, some people refuse to believe his stories.
meta.bible: Marco Polo: Venetian merchant and traveller, born about 1254, died in January 1324; curious, careful and observant. Niccolò Polo: Marco's father, a merchant. Maffeo Polo: Marco's uncle, a merchant. Kublai Khan: the Great Khan, ruler of the Mongol empire and of China. Mongol: the people of the Khan. Rustichello of Pisa: a writer of romances who wrote down Marco's stories in a Genoese prison. Teobaldo: a church leader at Acre who became Pope in 1271. Kokachin: a seventeen-year-old Mongol princess sent to marry Arghun. Arghun: the Mongol ruler of Persia, who died before she arrived. Ghazan: Arghun's son, whom she married. Donata: Marco's wife. Venice: the trading city on the lagoon where Marco was born. Genoa: Venice's rival; the city of the prison. Curzola: the island where the sea battle of 1298 took place. Constantinople. Acre. Jerusalem. Ayas. Ararat. Caspian. Baghdad. Tabriz. Persia. Saveh. Kerman. Hormuz. Badakhshan. Afghanistan. Pamir. Kashgar. Yarkand. Khotan. Silk Road. Lop. Dunhuang. Ganzhou. Shangdu: the Khan's summer capital, Xanadu. Khanbaliq: the Khan's winter capital, now Beijing. Yunnan. Yangzhou. Yangtze. Grand Canal. Hangzhou: called Quinsai, the City of Heaven. Zaiton: now Quanzhou, a great port. Cipangu: Japan, which Marco never visited. Sumatra. Ceylon: now Sri Lanka. Adam's Peak. India. Trebizond. Black Sea. Mediterranean. Fra Mauro: a Venetian mapmaker of the 1450s. Christopher Columbus. Il Milione: Marco's nickname. Description of the World: the book's own title; it is also called The Travels of Marco Polo. Noah. Buddha. Buddhists. Muslims. Beijing. Quanzhou. Sri Lanka. Marco Polo's sheep: a wild sheep with long horns. Voice and tone: wonder and curiosity, plain and clear; accurate; Marco reports what he saw and what he heard, and the retelling says plainly when something is a story, a doubt or an exaggeration; no gore. NEW NAMES AND FACTS FOR THE FULL BOOK. Muslin: fine cotton cloth named after Mosul. Soldaia: Sudak in the Crimea. Crimea. Berke: a Mongol ruler on the Volga, a grandson of Genghis Khan. Volga. Genghis Khan: founder of the Mongol empire, grandfather of Kublai. Bukhara: a great trading city in Central Asia. Hulagu: a Mongol ruler of Persia. Cogatal: a Mongol noble who set out with the brothers and fell ill. Clement: the Pope who died in 1268. Gregory: the name Teobaldo took as Pope. Nicholas and William: two friars who turned back. Baibars: the ruler of Egypt whose raids frightened the friars. Sivas. Erzurum. Turkey. Georgia. Derbent. Baku. Mosul. Mongols. Alexander. Magi. Wise Men. Yazd. Balkh. Wakhan. Taklamakan. Charchan. Pein. Lop. Dunhuang. Sachiu. Ganzhou. Campichu. Zhangye. Khotan. Samarkand. Alamut. Old Man of the Mountain. Mulehet. Gate. Tartar. Tartars. Kaidu. Nayan. Bayan. Xiangyang. Song. Mangi: Marco's name for south China. Fujian. Fuzhou. Tingiu. Dehua. Suzhou. West Lake. Phoenix Hill. Champa. Vietnam. Java. Pentam. Perlak. Ferlec. Andaman. Seilan. Maabar. Malabar. Gujarat. Mylapore. Thomas: the apostle, said to be buried near Mylapore. Peter. Ramusio: a Venetian editor who in the 1550s printed stories of Marco that are not in the earliest texts. Lamba Doria: the Genoese admiral at Curzola. Meloria. Pisa. Genoa. Arthur. Donata Badoer: Marco's wife. Fantina. Bellela. Moreta. San Giovanni Crisostomo. San Lorenzo. Corte del Milion. Pipino. Ming. Yuan. Rashid. Frances Wood. Marco Polo Bridge: Lugou Bridge near Beijing. Lugou. Pulisanghin. Taiyuan. Xi'an. Kenjanfu. Yellow River. Sichuan. Tibet. Yunnan. Karajan. Vochan. Mien. Burma. Daidu. Green Mound. White Feast. Kumis. Khanbaliq. Karakorum. Lop desert. Eve. Adam. Sakyamuni. Moses. Muhammad. Jesus. Easter. Constantinople.
chapters: A Boy Whose Father Was Away
The Tombs of the Wise Men
Errands to the Edge of the Empire

beats.scene: Venice at dawn: boats, canals and merchants unloading cloth and spices
beats.summary: Marco Polo is born in Venice, a rich trading city, while his father and uncle are far away.

beats.scene: Narrow canals, small boats and tall merchant houses along a Venetian waterfront
beats.summary: Venice is a city of islands and canals whose wealth comes from trade by sea.

beats.scene: Two merchants look at jewels in a busy market of Constantinople
beats.summary: Niccolò and Maffeo trade in Constantinople and then decide to travel further east with jewels.

beats.scene: Two riders cross a wide grass plain towards a camp of tents
beats.summary: The brothers sail to the Crimea and ride to the camp of Berke, a Mongol ruler on the Volga.

beats.scene: A Mongol ruler in a rich tent looks at a tray of sparkling jewels
beats.summary: Berke is delighted with the jewels and pays the brothers more than they asked.

beats.scene: Two merchants and a pack horse stand on a road closed by armed riders
beats.summary: War between Berke and Hulagu closes the road home, so the brothers go east to Bukhara.

beats.scene: Two Venetians in rich robes sit in the courtyard of a Bukhara house
beats.summary: The brothers wait three years in Bukhara for the road to open.

beats.scene: Persian envoys on horses stop at a Bukhara house to talk to two merchants
beats.summary: Envoys of Hulagu invite the brothers to visit the Great Khan, who has never met a European.

beats.scene: A line of riders and pack animals crosses a high snowy pass
beats.summary: The brothers travel with the envoys for a year, across mountains and plains, to the Great Khan.

beats.scene: Kublai Khan sits on a golden seat and smiles at two Venetians
beats.summary: Kublai Khan welcomes the two Venetians kindly.

beats.scene: Kublai Khan listens while the brothers describe kings and cities far to the west
beats.summary: Kublai asks the brothers about the kings and the lands of Europe.

beats.scene: The Khan studies a drawing of a church, while the brothers point west
beats.summary: Kublai asks about the Pope and the Christian church, which he knows little about.

beats.scene: The Khan hands a roll of paper and a tablet to the two brothers
beats.summary: Kublai decides to send the brothers back to Europe as his own messengers.

beats.scene: A scribe writes a long letter in a tent while the Khan watches
beats.summary: The Khan writes to the Pope and asks for a hundred wise Christian teachers.

beats.scene: A small brass lamp burns in a holy place, with a flask beside it
beats.summary: The Khan also asks for holy oil from the lamp that burns at the tomb of Jesus in Jerusalem.

beats.scene: The Khan gives a golden tablet to the brothers in his hall
beats.summary: The Khan gives the brothers a golden tablet that lets them travel safely and get help.

beats.scene: A Mongol noble lies ill under a blanket as the brothers prepare to leave
beats.summary: Cogatal falls ill and is left behind, so the brothers go on alone.

beats.scene: Two travellers in wet cloaks cross a flooded plain and a rough road
beats.summary: The brothers take three years to reach the coast of Armenia, held up by bad weather and floods.

beats.scene: A church leader shakes his head as two travellers stand before him in Acre
beats.summary: In Acre the brothers learn that the Pope has died and that no new Pope has been chosen.

beats.scene: A tall teenage boy greets two tired travellers at a Venetian doorway
beats.summary: Around 1269 the brothers reach Venice, where Niccolò learns that his wife has died and meets his son Marco, now about fifteen.

beats.scene: Niccolò and Maffeo sit by a window in Venice, looking at the empty harbour
beats.summary: After two years without a new Pope, the brothers decide to go back to the Khan.

beats.scene: A young man in a travelling cloak says goodbye on a Venetian quay
beats.summary: In 1271 seventeen-year-old Marco leaves Venice with his father and uncle.

beats.scene: Three Venetians climb the stairs of a church-leader's house in Acre
beats.summary: At Acre the Polos ask Teobaldo's advice, and he gives them letters for the Khan.

beats.scene: Three travellers kneel in a quiet church in Jerusalem beside a burning lamp
beats.summary: The Polos go to Jerusalem and take a flask of holy oil for the Khan.

beats.scene: A rider on a tired horse reaches three travellers at a port in Armenia
beats.summary: At Ayas the Polos hear that Teobaldo has been chosen as Pope and is calling them back.

beats.scene: The new Pope hands a letter to the Polos beside two friars in grey
beats.summary: The new Pope sends two friars and a letter to the Khan, with the Polos.

beats.scene: Two friars in grey robes walk back along a road, away from distant fighting
beats.summary: The two friars turn back when fighting breaks out, and the Polos go on alone.

beats.scene: A caravan stops at a market with bright carpets and silk for sale
beats.summary: In Turkey the Polos pass through towns where fine carpets and silk are made.

beats.scene: Three riders climb a cold, snowy road between high bare hills in Armenia
beats.summary: The Polos cross the high lands of Armenia in cold weather, passing through Erzurum.

beats.scene: A snowy mountain with a flat white peak rises above a green valley
beats.summary: Marco sees Mount Ararat, where people say that Noah's boat came to rest.

beats.scene: A caravan passes through a narrow gate between a steep mountain and the sea
beats.summary: In Georgia the road runs through a narrow pass said to have been closed by Alexander the Great.

beats.scene: Camels carry barrels from a black oil spring near the Caspian shore
beats.summary: Near Baku, Marco sees a spring of oil that flows without stopping and is used for lamps and medicine.

beats.scene: Weavers work at looms in a dusty town near a wide, slow river
beats.summary: At Mosul the Polos see fine cloth, which we still call muslin, being made.

beats.scene: A city of domes and towers stands on a river with a boat bridge
beats.summary: At Baghdad Marco sees the old home of the caliphs, a city taken by the Mongols in 1258.

beats.scene: A man prays on a hillside as a mountain seems to move behind him
beats.summary: In Baghdad Marco is told a story of a one-eyed cobbler whose faith moved a mountain.

beats.scene: Merchants from many lands argue over silk and pearls in a crowded Tabriz bazaar
beats.summary: At Tabriz in Persia the Polos find a rich trading city where merchants from India, Europe and China meet.

beats.scene: A trader weighs a pearl on a small scale while a young Venetian watches
beats.summary: Marco watches the traders of Tabriz closely and learns how they make their profits.

beats.scene: Fine horses stand in a line at a market while buyers inspect their legs
beats.summary: Marco hears that the best horses of Persia are sold in India for high prices.

beats.scene: Camels rest at night outside a walled inn in the desert
beats.summary: Caravans stop at night at walled inns, where travellers and animals can rest safely.

beats.scene: An official bows to a golden tablet and orders fresh horses for the Polos
beats.summary: Wherever the Polos show the Khan's golden tablet, officials give them horses, food and guides.

beats.scene: Three old men in rich robes lie in three tombs in a Persian town
beats.summary: At Saveh, Marco is shown the tombs of the Three Wise Men of the Christmas story.

beats.scene: A small burning fire sits in a stone temple while visitors watch in silence
beats.summary: Marco hears a local story about how the Wise Men's gifts led to a sacred fire that never goes out.

beats.scene: A merchant touches rolls of coloured silk in the market of Yazd
beats.summary: Marco passes through Yazd, a good city on the way, known for its silk cloth.

beats.scene: Armed riders appear on a dusty plain as three travellers hurry to a fort
beats.summary: Marco tells how raiders called Caraunas attacked travellers, and how he escaped to a village.

beats.scene: A craftsman cuts a bright blue stone in a workshop in Kerman
beats.summary: In Kerman, Marco sees mines of turquoise and fine steel work, saddles and embroidery.

beats.scene: Travellers bend against a hot wind as they descend a dry, stony slope
beats.summary: The Polos descend from Kerman to the hot plain near the sea, where the heat is fierce.

beats.scene: A harbour at Hormuz with ships unloading pearls, spices and horses
beats.summary: The Polos reach the port of Hormuz, where ships bring spices, pearls and silk from India.

beats.scene: A small wooden boat held together with rope floats in a harbour
beats.summary: The Polos see that the ships of Hormuz are sewn together with rope, and decide not to sail in them.

beats.scene: A small group of travellers walks through a dry salt desert at sunset
beats.summary: The Polos turn back north and cross a salt desert where water is scarce and bitter.

beats.scene: A hidden garden with fountains and flowers beyond a stone wall in the mountains
beats.summary: On the road Marco hears the tale of the Old Man of the Mountain and his secret garden.

beats.scene: Broken walls of a great old city stand on a plain beneath distant mountains
beats.summary: The Polos pass through Balkh, once a noble city, which the Mongols had ruined.

beats.scene: A sick young man rests in a stone house while mountains shine outside
beats.summary: Marco falls ill in Badakhshan and recovers there after about a year in the clean mountain air.

beats.scene: A king's servant shows a glowing red stone and a deep blue stone
beats.summary: Marco describes Badakhshan's rubies, blue lapis lazuli and salt, and says the king guards the best stones.

beats.scene: A narrow path climbs beside a rushing river towards snowy peaks
beats.summary: The Polos climb a long valley towards the high Pamir mountains.

beats.scene: A traveller holds a pot over a small fire on a windy plateau
beats.summary: Marco notes that no birds fly on the high Pamir and that fire does not burn as strongly or cook as well.

beats.scene: A wild sheep with huge curved horns stands on a rocky mountain slope
beats.summary: Marco describes a wild sheep with huge horns, which is now called Marco Polo's sheep.

beats.scene: A small party walks slowly through a vast empty valley with no houses
beats.summary: The crossing of the Pamir takes twelve days, with no houses or grass, so the Polos carry all their food.

beats.scene: A green oasis with orchards and cotton fields appears beyond a stony desert
beats.summary: At Kashgar the Polos reach green gardens, cotton fields and a town of merchants who travel far.

beats.scene: A caravan crosses a shallow river beside a dusty oasis town
beats.summary: At Yarkand Marco notes that many people have swollen throats, which he blames on the water.

beats.scene: Workers search a shallow river bed for smooth white stones of jade
beats.summary: At Khotan, Marco learns that the river beds hold the jade that Chinese craftsmen prize.

beats.scene: Mud-brick houses stand at the edge of a huge empty desert of sand
beats.summary: Beyond Khotan the Polos pass small towns at the edge of the great sand desert.

beats.scene: Camels kneel while men fill leather bags with water at a desert town
beats.summary: At Lop travellers rest for a week and load animals with food before crossing the desert.

beats.scene: A line of camels crosses wide sand dunes under a hot, white sky
beats.summary: The crossing takes about a month, with water in wells that are far apart and sometimes bitter.

beats.scene: A lone traveller stops in the sand and turns to look behind him
beats.summary: Marco writes that travellers who fall behind may hear voices calling their names and wander away.

beats.scene: A night caravan camp where drums sound in the dark beside the tents
beats.summary: Marco says the desert spirits sometimes sound like musical instruments and drums, which the travellers feared.

beats.scene: People burn paper models of horses and servants at a funeral
beats.summary: At Dunhuang the Polos see people burning paper horses and servants so the dead will have them in the next life.

beats.scene: A temple with a golden roof and monks in yellow robes ringing a bell
beats.summary: Marco meets Buddhist monks in temples and learns something about Buddha and the worship of idols.

beats.scene: A large city with a church, a mosque and a temple side by side
beats.summary: At Ganzhou the Polos stay about a year in a city where Christians, Muslims and Buddhists live together.

beats.scene: A huge golden Buddha lies on its side in a dim temple hall
beats.summary: At Ganzhou Marco sees great statues, some lying down and covered with gold, with many smaller ones around them.

beats.scene: Riders in bright Mongol coats arrive with horses to welcome the Polos
beats.summary: The Khan sends messengers forty days' ride to meet the Polos and bring them to his court.

beats.scene: A white marble palace and a green walled park under a bright summer sky
beats.summary: After forty days the Polos reach Shangdu, the Khan's summer capital, where a marble palace stands in a vast park.

beats.scene: Deer, cranes and falcons move through a fenced park of meadows and streams
beats.summary: Marco describes the wall around the park, which holds streams, meadows and animals for the Khan to hunt.

beats.scene: A golden cane palace stands among trees, tied down with long silk cords
beats.summary: Marco describes a palace of gilded bamboo that can be taken apart and carried, held up by silk cords.

beats.scene: Two older Venetians and a young man bow before the seated Khan
beats.summary: Niccolò and Maffeo present Marco to the Khan, who welcomes the young man kindly.

beats.scene: The Khan takes a small flask and papers from a bowing Venetian
beats.summary: The Polos give the Khan the holy oil from Jerusalem and the letters from the Pope's representative.

beats.scene: A long table of lords eating and drinking in a great tent hall
beats.summary: The Khan holds a great feast to celebrate the arrival of the Polos.

beats.scene: A young man studies strange writing beside a Chinese teacher
beats.summary: Marco quickly learns four languages and their scripts, which makes him useful at court.

beats.scene: A young traveller in a long coat rides from the palace with a servant
beats.summary: The Khan sends Marco on a mission to a far country, and Marco prepares carefully for it.

beats.scene: Marco tells the Khan about strange customs as the ruler listens closely
beats.summary: Marco returns and tells the Khan everything about the customs and wonders of the land he visited.

beats.scene: Marco, in rich robes, stands among Chinese officials at a palace gate
beats.summary: Marco becomes a trusted servant of the Khan and serves him for about seventeen years.

beats.scene: Builders and carts on a wide plain beside a rising new city
beats.summary: Kublai Khan has built Khanbaliq, a new capital beside an older city, and moves the court there for the winter.

beats.scene: A great square wall with twelve gates stands around a city of roofs
beats.summary: Marco describes the walls of Khanbaliq, square in shape, with twelve gates and a guard at each one.

beats.scene: A long straight street with shops and houses leads to a distant gate
beats.summary: The streets of Khanbaliq run so straight that a man standing at one gate can see the gate at the other end.

beats.scene: A watchman strikes a great bell in a tower as night falls
beats.summary: At night a great bell rings and no one may go out, except for a good reason such as a woman in labour or an illness.

beats.scene: A vast palace courtyard with a long marble stair and a great hall
beats.summary: The Khan's palace stands inside four walls, with a great hall big enough for six thousand people to eat.

beats.scene: A palace roof shines in red, green, blue and yellow tiles under the sun
beats.summary: The palace roof is covered with tiles of red, green, blue and yellow that shine like glass and can be seen from far away.

beats.scene: A tall green hill covered with trees beside a palace and a lake
beats.summary: The Khan has built an earth hill covered with evergreen trees beside the palace, called the Green Mound.

beats.scene: Swans and fish in a palace lake, with a stone bridge and palace buildings
beats.summary: The Khan's park has a lake full of fish, a stone bridge and animals such as white deer.

beats.scene: Merchants with carts of silk and goods enter a great city gate
beats.summary: Merchants from all countries bring goods to Khanbaliq, and Marco says a thousand cartloads of silk arrive every day.

beats.scene: Astrologers in long robes study the sky with strange instruments on a tower
beats.summary: The Khan keeps about five thousand astrologers, Christian, Muslim and Chinese, who study the sky and make the calendar.

beats.scene: Workers strip bark from mulberry trees outside a Khanbaliq mint
beats.summary: Marco visits the Khan's mint and learns that his money is made of paper from the bark of the mulberry tree.

beats.scene: Officials stamp a red seal on rectangles of dark paper at a long table
beats.summary: The paper is cut into pieces of different sizes, and officials sign them and press the Khan's red seal on each one.

beats.scene: A merchant hands a bag of pearls to an official and receives paper notes
beats.summary: Merchants who bring gold, pearls and jewels to the Khan are paid in paper, and everyone accepts the notes.

beats.scene: A traveller offers coins to a shopkeeper who refuses and points to paper notes
beats.summary: Everyone in the empire must accept the notes, and anyone who refuses may be punished.

beats.scene: A clerk swaps a torn note for a clean new one at a desk
beats.summary: When a note becomes worn or torn, the owner can exchange it for a new one at the mint, for a small fee.

beats.scene: Carts loaded with black rocks come down from a mountain to the city
beats.summary: Marco notices that people in Khanbaliq burn black stones dug from the mountains instead of wood.

beats.scene: Steam rises from a public bath house in a snowy street
beats.summary: The people of Khanbaliq heat their baths with the stones and bathe often, which Marco finds remarkable.

beats.scene: A rider with bells on his belt gallops to a snowy post house
beats.summary: Marco describes the post stations along the roads, where messengers change horses on the way to the Khan.

beats.scene: A messenger with a belt of small bells rides hard along a road
beats.summary: Messengers wear belts with bells so people can hear them coming, and they can ride about two hundred miles in a day.

beats.scene: A road lined with tall green trees, and grain stores beyond
beats.summary: The Khan plants trees along the roads for shade and keeps stores of grain to feed the poor in hard years.

beats.scene: Lords in matching gold robes bow before the Khan on his birthday
beats.summary: On the Khan's birthday in late September, thousands of lords wear matching robes and bring him gifts.

beats.scene: Everyone at court wears white and bows as a white horse is led forward
beats.summary: At the Chinese New Year in February the Khan holds the White Feast, where everyone wears white for good luck.

beats.scene: Elephants and camels in rich cloths walk in a long parade past the palace
beats.summary: On the day of the feast people bring the Khan gifts, often white horses, and a parade of elephants and camels passes the palace.

beats.scene: The Khan sits at a raised table above long rows of guests
beats.summary: In the great hall the Khan sits at a raised table, and his guests sit at lower tables, in order of rank.

beats.scene: Servants with silk cloths over their mouths carry dishes to the Khan
beats.summary: Servants who serve the Khan cover their mouths and noses with silk so that their breath does not touch his food.

beats.scene: Mongol riders gallop across a plain, carrying small bags of dried milk
beats.summary: Mongol soldiers ride for days with little food, living on mare's milk and dried milk paste that they carry with them.

beats.scene: White mares graze on the grass while a rider pours milk on the ground
beats.summary: The Khan keeps a great herd of white mares whose milk only his family may drink, and he pours milk on the ground for the spirits.

beats.scene: Riders with falcons on their wrists leave a camp at dawn
beats.summary: In spring the Khan goes hunting with thousands of men, falconers and trained dogs, and Marco rides with the party.

beats.scene: A wooden house on four elephants moves across a plain with hunters beside it
beats.summary: The Khan travels on the hunt in a wooden pavilion carried by four elephants, with a bed inside and gold cloth outside.

beats.scene: A huge tent camp spreads across a plain like a town, with banners flying
beats.summary: The Khan's hunting camp is like a city of tents, and the Khan's own tent is big enough for a thousand knights.

beats.scene: Marco writes in a small notebook beside his horse on a dusty road
beats.summary: Marco travels on the Khan's business to far provinces and keeps notes of everything he sees.

beats.scene: Vines grow on a hillside above a town with smoking iron workshops
beats.summary: In Taiyuan Marco finds vineyards that make wine, which is sold across the land, and workshops for iron and weapons.

beats.scene: A long stone bridge with carved marble lions crosses a wide river
beats.summary: Marco describes the great stone bridge over a river near Khanbaliq, with marble lions and many arches.

beats.scene: A busy walled city with silk workshops and a palace of a Mongol prince
beats.summary: Marco visits Xi'an, a rich city of silk and gold, where a son of the Khan rules in a fine palace.

beats.scene: Mountain trails run beside a deep river towards a town with a roofed bridge
beats.summary: In the mountains of Sichuan, Marco crosses deep valleys and reaches Chengdu, with a great bridge covered by a roof.

beats.scene: Green bamboo canes crack and burst in a fire while a horse shies
beats.summary: Marco describes how green bamboo canes burst with a loud bang when burned, frightening horses and strangers.

beats.scene: A traveller holds a small pouch of musk beside tall, snowy mountains
beats.summary: On the edge of Tibet, Marco hears of the musk deer, whose scent is used in perfumes, and of salt used as money.

beats.scene: A long, scaly crocodile lies on a muddy bank beside a slow river
beats.summary: In Yunnan, Marco sees crocodiles that he calls great serpents with jaws wide enough to swallow a man.

beats.scene: A smiling man shows a mouth of golden teeth beside a table of shells
beats.summary: In Yunnan some people cover their teeth with thin gold caps and use small white shells as money.

beats.scene: Mongol archers shoot at tall war elephants carrying wooden towers in a forest
beats.summary: Marco tells how in 1277 a Mongol army beat the elephants of the king of Burma by tying its horses to trees and shooting arrows.

beats.scene: A map of a rich southern land of rivers, rice fields and walled cities
beats.summary: South China, which Marco calls Mangi, is a rich land ruled by the Song, and Kublai wants it for his empire.

beats.scene: Stone walls and moats of a great river fortress stand against a Mongol army
beats.summary: The city of Xiangyang holds out against the Mongols for about five years before it falls.

beats.scene: Three Venetians watch workers build a huge throwing machine beside a wall
beats.summary: Marco says his father and uncle helped build stone-throwing machines that broke the siege, but this is probably wrong.

beats.scene: The Mongol general Bayan sits on a horse beside a map of rivers
beats.summary: The Khan's general Bayan leads the great army south, and Marco says his name means Hundred Eyes.

beats.scene: A river so wide that its far bank cannot be seen, crowded with ships
beats.summary: Marco describes the Yangtze as so wide that it looks like a sea, with more ships than all the rivers of Europe together.

beats.scene: A small emperor in a golden robe sits beside a woman and officials
beats.summary: In 1276 Hangzhou surrenders to Bayan, and the child emperor goes north; the city is spared.

beats.scene: Marco in official robes sits in a hall in Yangzhou with clerks beside him
beats.summary: Marco says that he governed Yangzhou for three years, though Chinese records do not name him.

beats.scene: Workers rake salt from shallow pools by the sea beside piles of white salt
beats.summary: Marco learns that the salt works near Yangzhou bring the Khan an enormous income in taxes.

beats.scene: A deep canal with stone banks and a stream of loaded barges
beats.summary: Marco sees the Grand Canal, which carries rice, silk and other goods between the south and the capital.

beats.scene: Hundreds of boats with sails and oars pass under a canal town bridge
beats.summary: At the towns along the canal, so many boats pass that no one can count them, and Marco thinks of Venice.

beats.scene: A vast city of curved roofs seen from a hill, beside a bright lake
beats.summary: Marco reaches Hangzhou, which he calls Quinsai, a name he says means City of Heaven.

beats.scene: A broad city wall seen from a boat, with a lake on one side
beats.summary: Marco says the city is about a hundred miles around, with a great lake on one side and a wide river on the other.

beats.scene: A tall stone bridge arches over a canal as a ship passes beneath
beats.summary: Marco says there are twelve thousand stone bridges in the city, and the bridges are so high that ships pass beneath them.

beats.scene: Ten huge market squares crowded with shoppers beside tall stone warehouses
beats.summary: The city has ten great market squares, with stone warehouses, and merchants sell fish, meat, fruit and spices.

beats.scene: Paved streets with many small shops, each making a different craft
beats.summary: The streets are paved with stone and brick, and twelve craft guilds each have twelve thousand workshops.

beats.scene: A house door with a small wooden plate beside a clerk writing
beats.summary: Each house has a tablet with the names of everyone who lives there, and innkeepers write down the names of their guests.

beats.scene: A calm lake with willows and small boats under a bright blue sky
beats.summary: On the west side of the city lies a beautiful lake, with gardens and palaces on its shores.

beats.scene: Painted pleasure boats with silk awnings drift on a lake
beats.summary: Rich people hire painted pleasure boats for feasts on the lake, and Marco says nothing is more delightful.

beats.scene: An old palace with many halls and gardens stands behind high white walls
beats.summary: The old palace of the Song kings is still there, with many halls and a large garden, and the Khan's officer guards it.

beats.scene: Guards stand on a bridge at night near a stone tower
beats.summary: At night guards watch the bridges and the streets, and stone towers keep goods safe from the fires that often break out.

beats.scene: A mule train climbs through green hills and bamboo towards the south coast
beats.summary: From Hangzhou Marco travels south through hills, rivers and many towns into the province of Fujian.

beats.scene: Ginger roots and sugar loaves are stacked on a market table in Fuzhou
beats.summary: In Fuzhou Marco finds cheap ginger and galangal and learns how people there make sugar.

beats.scene: Workers shape white bowls and dishes beside a kiln in a small town
beats.summary: At Tingiu, now Dehua, Marco finds workshops that make bowls and dishes of porcelain, which are very cheap.

beats.scene: A great harbour crowded with tall ships and busy docks at sunrise
beats.summary: Marco reaches Zaiton, now Quanzhou, which he says is one of the two greatest ports in the world.

beats.scene: Sacks of pepper are carried off a great ship while officials count them
beats.summary: Marco says that for every ship of pepper sent to Egypt for Christian lands, a hundred ships arrive at Zaiton; the Khan takes a share.

beats.scene: Merchants from many lands trade among temples and mosques in a harbour town
beats.summary: Merchants from India, Persia and many other lands live in Zaiton, and the city has temples, churches and mosques.

beats.scene: A huge wooden ship with four masts and a high deck sails into harbour
beats.summary: Marco describes the Chinese sea ships, which are made of fir wood with double planks and four masts.

beats.scene: A cutaway view of a ship's hull divided into thirteen watertight rooms
beats.summary: The hulls are divided into thirteen watertight compartments, so that a leak in one part will not sink the ship.

beats.scene: Sailors tend small vegetable tubs on the deck of a large ship
beats.summary: The big ships carry as many as three hundred sailors, small boats and even tubs of vegetables growing on the deck.

beats.scene: A golden palace roof shines on a distant island beyond grey stormy waves
beats.summary: Marco hears about Japan, an island far to the east where, he is told, the palace roof is covered with gold.

beats.scene: Broken ships and floating wood in a storm near a rocky island coast
beats.summary: Marco says the Khan twice sent fleets against Japan, but storms destroyed them and few men came home.

beats.scene: Two older merchants look out of a palace window with worried faces
beats.summary: After many years the Polos want to go home, but they fear what will happen after the old Khan dies.

beats.scene: The old Khan shakes his head while a young Venetian stands before him
beats.summary: Niccolò asks the Khan to let them go, but the Khan, who is fond of them, refuses more than once.

beats.scene: Three envoys in Persian robes bow before the Khan in a great hall
beats.summary: Envoys from Arghun, the Mongol ruler of Persia, arrive at the court to ask for a new wife for their king.

beats.scene: A young woman in a silk robe stands calmly before the Khan
beats.summary: The Khan chooses a girl of seventeen named Kokachin, beautiful and clever, as the bride for Arghun.

beats.scene: Marco in sea clothes stands at a harbour beside a ship from India
beats.summary: War has closed the land road, but Marco has just come back from India by sea, and the envoys ask the Khan to let the Polos guide them.

beats.scene: The old Khan hands a golden tablet and sealed letters to Niccolò
beats.summary: The Khan, though unwilling, agrees, and gives the Polos golden tablets and letters for the Pope and kings of Europe.

beats.scene: Fourteen ships with red sails and tall masts wait in a crowded harbour
beats.summary: A fleet of fourteen big ships is made ready, with about six hundred passengers and enough supplies for two years.

beats.scene: A princess and three Venetians wave farewell from the stern of a ship
beats.summary: In about 1291 the fleet leaves Zaiton with the princess, the envoys and the three Polos on board.

beats.scene: An elephant stands beside a wooden pier in a hot, green southern harbour
beats.summary: After three months at sea the fleet reaches Champa, whose king pays the Khan a yearly gift of elephants.

beats.scene: Ships sail past a green island with tall mountains and clouds of spice smoke
beats.summary: The fleet sails past Java, which sailors call the richest island in the world, and then through the narrow channels near Pentam.

beats.scene: Tired sailors look at a calm, windless sea beside a green tropical shore
beats.summary: At Sumatra the monsoon winds are wrong, and the fleet has to wait about five months before it can sail on.

beats.scene: Men build a wooden fort with a ditch and towers on a tropical beach
beats.summary: The travellers build a wooden fort for safety, buy food from the local people and see palm wine and sago trees.

beats.scene: A grey rhinoceros wallows in mud, with a black horn on its nose
beats.summary: In Sumatra Marco sees a creature he calls a unicorn, which is really a rhinoceros, and is not at all as beautiful as the stories say.

beats.scene: A mosque stands beside a small harbour on the north coast of an island
beats.summary: In the town of Perlak, Muslim traders have taught the people their faith, which shows how religion travels with trade.

beats.scene: A green island with a mountain and a king holding a huge red jewel
beats.summary: At Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, Marco hears about the king's great ruby, which the Khan once tried to buy.

beats.scene: Pilgrims climb a steep mountain using iron chains on the rock
beats.summary: Marco hears about Adam's Peak, where pilgrims climb with the help of chains to see a footprint that different faiths explain in different ways.

beats.scene: Divers with stones tied to their legs plunge from a boat into green water
beats.summary: Off the south coast of India, divers search for pearls, and men called charmers say they keep the sharks away.

beats.scene: A small white church stands beside the sea near a crowd of pilgrims
beats.summary: At Mylapore, on the south-east coast of India, Marco finds a church where Saint Thomas, one of Jesus' friends, is believed to be buried.

beats.scene: Sacks of pepper and ginger beside the harbour as ships with torn sails pass
beats.summary: Along the Malabar coast, Marco sees the pepper gardens and learns of pirates who attack the passing ships.

beats.scene: A thin, tired crowd steps off a ship onto a hot harbour in Persia
beats.summary: After about two years at sea the fleet reaches Hormuz in about 1293, and Marco says that most of the passengers have died on the way.

beats.scene: A princess in a silk robe hears sad news from an envoy
beats.summary: Arghun has died, and the Polos find his brother Gaikhatu ruling as regent, so they ask what should be done with the princess.

beats.scene: A young prince and a princess stand together while her friends say farewell
beats.summary: Gaikhatu says that Kokachin should marry Arghun's son Ghazan, and she weeps when the Polos say goodbye.

beats.scene: Three travellers rest in a Persian courtyard while a servant brings food
beats.summary: The Polos rest for some months in Tabriz, and Gaikhatu gives them golden tablets for safe travel to the West.

beats.scene: A harbour with Genoese and Greek ships beneath a tall fortress on a hill
beats.summary: The Polos leave Tabriz and ride to Trebizond on the Black Sea, where they find ships for the voyage across it.

beats.scene: A great city of domes and walls on a strait seen from a ship
beats.summary: The Polos sail across the Black Sea and reach Constantinople, and from there they take ship for Venice.

beats.scene: Three weathered men in worn clothes stand on a quay in the Venice lagoon
beats.summary: In 1295, after about twenty-four years, the three Polos arrive in Venice, rich in jewels but poor in clothes.

beats.scene: A family stares from a Venetian doorway at three strangers in rough coats
beats.summary: At the family house the relatives do not recognise the travellers, and they speak Venetian with an odd accent.

beats.scene: A man slits a worn coat lining, and a pile of jewels falls out
beats.summary: A later story says the Polos held a feast, then cut open their old coats to show the jewels sewn inside; this tale was added by later storytellers.

beats.scene: A narrow Venetian courtyard with an old house and a stone well
beats.summary: The people of Venice nickname Marco Il Milione, and a courtyard in the city is still called the Corte del Milion.

beats.scene: Two fleets of galleys face each other across a wide blue sea
beats.summary: Venice and Genoa are rivals at sea, and in the 1290s they go to war once more.

beats.scene: A Venetian galley under oars leaves port with a red banner and armed men
beats.summary: Marco, according to old tradition, pays for a galley and joins the Venetian fleet, though the records are not clear.

beats.scene: Burning ships and broken oars on dark water under a crowded sky
beats.summary: In September 1298, in a battle near Curzola, the Genoese admiral Lamba Doria defeats the Venetian fleet and takes thousands of prisoners.

beats.scene: A prisoner stands in a narrow stone cell with a barred window
beats.summary: Marco is taken to Genoa as a prisoner, and he must wait there while the two cities argue about peace.

beats.scene: Two men sit at a rough table in a prison cell with papers
beats.summary: In the prison Marco meets a writer from Pisa named Rustichello, who has been a prisoner since an earlier sea battle.

beats.scene: A prisoner speaks while a writer with a quill copies his words on paper
beats.summary: Marco tells his story aloud, and Rustichello writes it down, probably with the help of Marco's own notes.

beats.scene: The first page of a hand-written book with a coloured capital letter
beats.summary: The book is written in French, and its opening words, like those of a romance, call on emperors, kings and all who want to learn about the world.

beats.scene: Pages show lists of cities, roads, prices and notes about customs and wonders
beats.summary: The book describes places, people, customs and animals, and it says when something is only a story that Marco has heard.

beats.scene: A prison door opens and a thin man steps out into the bright sunlight
beats.summary: In 1299 peace is made between Genoa and Venice, and Marco is set free and goes home.

beats.scene: A family sits at a long table with a woman and three small girls
beats.summary: Marco marries Donata Badoer, has three daughters and lives as a merchant in Venice, near the church of San Giovanni Crisostomo.

beats.scene: A monk copies a thick book by hand in a candlelit room
beats.summary: Without printing, the book spreads only by hand-copied versions in French, Latin, Italian and other languages.

beats.scene: A reader frowns over a page while two friends argue beside a candle
beats.summary: Some readers believe every word of the book, but many think that Marco has exaggerated, and they call it a book of marvels and numbers.

beats.scene: A scholar frowns over a list of things Marco never mentions
beats.summary: Critics ask why Marco does not mention tea, chopsticks or the Great Wall, though he spent seventeen years in China.

beats.scene: Scholars weigh an old book against a short list of missing things
beats.summary: Defenders reply that the Great Wall of that day was not the stone wall we know, that Marco used Persian names, and that his details of money, coal and the post are correct.

beats.scene: An old man in bed signs a paper beside his family and a priest
beats.summary: In January 1324 Marco makes a will in Venice, leaving money to his daughters and freeing a servant named Peter, a Tartar.

beats.scene: An old man in bed talks quietly with friends and a priest
beats.summary: A well-known story says that friends asked Marco on his deathbed to take back his stories, but he said he had not told half of what he had seen.

beats.scene: A great round map of the world with islands and names in old Italian
beats.summary: In the 1450s a Venetian monk named Fra Mauro draws a great world map that uses Marco's names for many places in Asia.

beats.scene: A sailor studies a book full of notes in the margins beside a map
beats.summary: Christopher Columbus owns a printed copy of Marco's book and writes notes in its margins, and he sails west hoping to reach Asia.

beats.scene: Two travellers on a mountain road look at a Jesuit's map of China
beats.summary: Later travellers follow Marco's road, and in the early 1600s Europeans prove that Cathay, the land in his book, is the same China that they know.

beats.scene: A reader sits with a book beside a Venice canal at sunset
beats.summary: Today the Travels is read all over the world, and the airport of Venice carries the name of Marco Polo.

A1A2: Marco Polo was born in Venice, a rich city on the water.
In Venice, many streets were canals, so people went about by boat.
In Constantinople, the brothers bought jewels to sell in far countries.
They sailed across the Black Sea and rode to a Mongol camp.
The ruler loved the jewels and paid the brothers a fair price.
Then war began, and the way back to Venice was closed.
The brothers waited in Bukhara for three years, but the road stayed closed.
Messengers going to the Great Khan invited the brothers to come along.
The journey took a whole year, across mountains and wide plains.
Kublai Khan welcomed the two Venetians with great kindness and honour.
The Khan asked many questions about kings and countries in Europe.
Next he asked about the Pope and the Christian church.
Kublai decided to send the brothers home as his own messengers.
The Khan wrote a letter asking the Pope to send a hundred wise men.
He also asked for oil from the holy lamp in Jerusalem.
The Khan gave them a golden tablet to protect them on the road.
Soon Cogatal fell ill and the brothers continued without him.
Rain, snow and floods made the journey last nearly three years.
In Acre they learned that the Pope had died.
In Venice, Niccolò learned that his wife had died.
No new Pope was chosen, so the brothers decided to go back.
In 1271 Marco, now seventeen, left Venice with his father and uncle.
In Acre, Teobaldo gave them a letter for the Khan.
They rode to Jerusalem and filled a small flask with holy oil.
At Ayas, news came that Teobaldo had become the new Pope.
The new Pope sent two church men, Nicholas and William, with them.
Nicholas and William grew afraid of the fighting and went back home.
In Turkey, the Polos saw beautiful carpets and fine silk cloth.
They climbed into cold, snowy mountains in Armenia.
Marco saw Mount Ararat, where people say Noah's boat stopped.
In Georgia, the road ran through a narrow pass beside the sea.
Near Baku, oil came out of the ground like a spring.
Near Mosul, people made the fine cloth called muslin.
Baghdad was once the home of the ruler of all Muslims.
In Baghdad, Marco heard a story about a man who moved a mountain.
In Tabriz, they found a huge market full of traders.
Marco watched the traders and learned how they made money.
In Persia, Marco saw fine horses that traders sold in India.
At night, the caravan stopped at an inn with strong walls.
Officials saw the golden tablet and quickly gave them fresh horses.
At Saveh, people showed Marco the tombs of the three Wise Men.
People there told him a story about a stone and a fire.
Yazd was a good city that made silk cloth.
Robbers attacked travellers on this road, but Marco escaped to a village.
In Kerman, people dug blue stones from the mountains and made fine saddles.
They went down to a hot plain near the sea.
At last they reached Hormuz, a busy port on the sea.
The Polos saw the weak boats and decided not to sail.
They crossed a dry desert where the water was bitter.
On the road, Marco heard a tale about the Old Man of the Mountain.
Balkh was once a great city, but the Mongols had broken it.
In Badakhshan, Marco became ill and stayed for almost a year.
Badakhshan had red stones, blue stones and silver in its mountains.
The road climbed beside a river towards very high mountains.
On the high plain, there were no birds and the fire was weak.
Marco saw wild sheep with very long, curved horns.
For twelve days, they found no houses and no grass.
Kashgar was green, with gardens and fields, after the dry hills.
In Yarkand, Marco saw many people with swollen throats and legs.
In Khotan, people found jade in the river and sold it.
Past Khotan, small towns stood at the edge of a huge desert.
At Lop, travellers rested and filled their bags with water.
The desert was so wide that the crossing took about a month.
A man who fell behind might hear voices calling his name.
At night, they sometimes heard drums and music in the empty desert.
In Dunhuang, people burned paper horses for the dead.
In the temples, Marco met monks and learned about Buddha.
In Ganzhou, they stayed for a year in a large, busy city.
Marco saw a giant statue that lay on its side.
The Khan sent messengers to meet the Polos on the road.
The Polos came to Shangdu, where the Khan spent each summer.
A tall wall ran round a park full of deer and birds.
Inside the park was a palace made of bamboo and gold.
Niccolò and Maffeo bowed to the Khan and showed him Marco.
The Polos gave the Khan the holy oil and the letters.
The Khan gave a great feast to welcome the three travellers.
Marco worked hard and soon learned four languages.
The Khan sent Marco on a long journey for the first time.
Marco came back and told the Khan everything he had seen.
Marco became a trusted servant of the Khan for many years.
In winter, the Khan moved to a new city called Khanbaliq.
The city was a perfect square with a tall wall around it.
The streets were so straight that you could see to the end.
At night a great bell rang, and people had to stay in.
The Khan's palace was the largest palace Marco had ever seen.
The roof had tiles in red, green, blue and yellow.
Next to the palace, the Khan had a hill made of earth.
The park had a lake, a stone bridge and many animals.
Merchants from many countries came to the city to buy and sell.
The Khan kept many wise men who studied the stars.
Marco visited the Khan's mint, where money was made from paper.
Officials cut the paper into pieces and stamped each one.
Merchants gave jewels to the Khan and took paper money.
Everyone in the empire had to accept the paper money.
Torn notes could be changed for new ones at the mint.
People in the city burned black stones instead of wood.
The people of the city kept clean and used hot baths.
Along every road stood post houses where riders changed horses.
Riders wore bells so everyone knew a messenger was coming.
The Khan planted trees along the roads and stored grain.
On the Khan's birthday, all the lords wore matching robes.
At New Year, everyone at court wore white for good luck.
A great parade of elephants and camels passed in front of the palace.
In the hall, the Khan sat high above all his guests.
The servants covered their mouths with silk so they would not breathe on the food.
The Khan's soldiers could ride for many days with little food.
The Khan owned a great herd of white horses.
Every spring, the Khan went hunting with many thousands of men.
The Khan rode in a wooden room carried by four elephants.
The Khan's hunting camp looked like a whole city of tents.
Marco travelled for the Khan and wrote down all he saw.
In Taiyuan, Marco saw vines, wine and busy iron workshops.
He crossed a long stone bridge with lions made of marble.
In Xi'an, Marco found rich merchants and a prince's palace.
The road went through mountains and deep, green river valleys.
When green bamboo burned, it burst with a very loud bang.
Near Tibet, Marco heard of a small deer that gave musk.
In Yunnan, Marco saw giant animals with big jaws and short legs.
Some people in Yunnan covered their teeth with gold.
A Mongol army met war elephants and drove them away.
South China was a rich land, and the Khan wanted it.
One strong walled city held out against the Mongols for years.
Marco says the Polos built machines to throw stones at the walls.
General Bayan led the Mongol army south down the great river.
The Yangtze was so wide that it looked like a sea.
In 1276, the Song capital gave up without a fight.
Marco says that he ruled the city of Yangzhou for three years.
Near Yangzhou, workers made salt from sea water in the sun.
Marco saw the Grand Canal, a long river dug by people.
So many boats went along the canal that no one could count them.
At last Marco came to Hangzhou, which he called Quinsai.
Marco said the city was huge, about a hundred miles around.
The city had thousands of bridges, so high that ships passed under.
Ten big market squares held shops full of food and goods.
The streets were paved, and every craft had its own shops.
Each house had a board with the names of everyone inside.
On one side of the city lay a very beautiful lake.
Rich people hired painted boats and held feasts on the lake.
The old palace of the Song kings was still standing.
At night, guards watched the streets and the bridges.
From Hangzhou, Marco went south into green hills and forests.
In Fuzhou, Marco saw ginger, spices and sugar for sale.
At Tingiu, workers made fine white bowls and dishes.
Marco reached Zaiton, one of the biggest ports in the world.
For every pepper ship in Egypt, a hundred came to Zaiton.
Merchants from many lands lived and traded in Zaiton.
The Chinese ships were much bigger than ships in Europe.
Inside the hull were walls that kept water in one place.
Sailors grew fresh vegetables in tubs on the big ships.
Marco heard about an island called Japan, full of gold.
The Khan sent ships to attack Japan, but storms sank many of them.
After many years, the Polos wanted to go home to Venice.
The Khan was fond of the Polos and said no.
Messengers arrived from Persia with a request for the Khan.
The Khan chose a girl named Kokachin to be Arghun's wife.
War closed the road, and Marco knew the way by sea.
The Khan agreed and gave them gold tablets and letters.
The Khan had fourteen big ships made ready for the voyage.
In about 1291, the ships left Zaiton and sailed away.
After three months, the ships reached a land called Champa.
The ships sailed past Java, an island famous for its spices.
At Sumatra, the winds were wrong, and the fleet had to wait.
The travellers built a wooden fort and bought food from the people.
On Sumatra, Marco saw a strange horned animal and called it a unicorn.
In Perlak, traders from Arabia had taught people a new faith.
In Ceylon, the king owned the biggest ruby in the world.
Pilgrims climbed a tall mountain with the help of chains.
Divers dived for pearls from small boats off the coast of India.
In Mylapore, Marco found a church where Saint Thomas was buried.
On the Malabar coast, Marco saw pepper, ginger and many ships.
After two years at sea, the ships reached Hormuz.
King Arghun had died, so the princess had no husband.
The princess married Arghun's son, a young prince named Ghazan.
The Polos rested for some months in the rich city of Tabriz.
From Tabriz, the Polos rode to Trebizond, a port by the Black Sea.
The Polos sailed to Constantinople and then on to Venice.
In 1295, the three Polos at last came back to Venice.
Their own family did not recognise them at the door.
A later story said they cut open old coats and jewels fell out.
People in Venice gave Marco a new name, Il Milione.
Venice and Genoa were rivals, and soon they went to war.
Marco paid for a ship and joined the Venetian fleet.
At the battle of Curzola, the Venetians lost to the Genoese.
Marco was taken to Genoa and put in prison.
In prison, Marco met a writer called Rustichello from Pisa.
Marco told his stories, and Rustichello wrote them down.
The book began by asking all curious people to read it.
The book described many cities, roads, goods and customs.
In 1299, peace came, and Marco was free to go home.
Marco married a woman named Donata, and they had three daughters.
People copied the book by hand, because there were no printers.
Some readers believed the book, but others did not.
Critics asked why the book says nothing about tea or Chinese food habits.
Others said that most of the book was clearly true.
In January 1324, Marco made his will and set a servant free.
A story says Marco said he had not told half of what he saw.
A monk in Venice drew a big world map using Marco's names.
Christopher Columbus read the book and wrote notes in the margins.
Later travellers followed Marco's road and found the places he described.
Today, people all over the world still read the Travels.
B1B2: Marco Polo was born in Venice around 1254, in a city of canals, boats and busy markets. His father Niccolò and his uncle Maffeo were merchants who had sailed far away, and Marco did not know his father.
Venice was built on islands in a shallow lagoon, and its people lived by trade. Ships left its harbour loaded with salt and cloth and came back with pepper, silk and stories from the East.
Niccolò and Maffeo Polo traded in Constantinople for several years. In about 1260 they bought a store of jewels and decided to carry them to lands further north and east.
From the port of Soldaia, in the Crimea, the brothers rode for many days across open grassland. At last they reached the camp of Berke, a Mongol ruler who was a grandson of Genghis Khan.
Berke welcomed the Venetians kindly and was delighted with their jewels. He paid them generously, and they stayed at his camp for a year, which was a great honour.

A war broke out between Berke and Hulagu, another Mongol ruler, and the road home became too dangerous. The brothers turned east instead and crossed a desert for seventeen days to reach Bukhara, a great trading city.
In Bukhara the Venetians waited for a chance to go home, but the fighting never stopped. They stayed for three years and probably continued to trade while they waited.
In Bukhara they met envoys of Hulagu, who were on their way to the court of the Great Khan. The envoys had never seen Europeans and told the brothers that the Khan would be delighted to meet them.

The trip took the brothers about a year, because snow, floods and bad weather sometimes forced the group to stop. They saw many wonders on the way, though Marco's book says little about them, since he was not there.
At last the brothers stood before Kublai Khan, the grandson of Genghis Khan and ruler of China and much of Asia. He received them with great kindness and was glad to see men from so far away.
Kublai wanted to know how the kings of Europe ruled their lands and how their armies fought. The brothers had learned the Mongol language, so they could answer him clearly and without help.

Kublai then asked about the Pope, the head of the Christian church, and about what Christians believed. He had never heard much about it and wanted to know whether it had anything to teach his people.
After many talks the Khan decided to send the two brothers back to Europe as his envoys. A Mongol noble named Cogatal would travel with them and would carry the Khan's letter to the Pope.

In his letter, the Khan asked the Pope to send a hundred learned men who could explain the Christian faith and the arts of Europe. If they showed that their faith was better than others, he said, he and his people might follow it.
The Khan also asked the brothers to bring oil from the lamp that burns at the tomb of Jesus in Jerusalem. He had heard that this oil was very holy and wanted to have some for himself.
Before they left, the Khan gave the brothers a golden tablet carved with his command. Anyone who saw it had to give them horses, food and guards, and nobody was allowed to harm them.
A short way into the journey, Cogatal became so sick that he could not go on. The brothers left him in a town to recover and continued alone with the Khan's golden tablet to protect them.
Rain, snow and swollen rivers slowed them so much that it took almost three years to reach the port of Ayas. They finally arrived in April 1269 and sailed for Acre.

At Acre they heard that Pope Clement had died the year before, and that the cardinals had not yet chosen a new Pope. A church leader named Teobaldo, who lived there, told them to wait for the election.
In Venice Niccolò found that his wife had died while he was away. His son Marco was now about fifteen years old, and the boy met his father for the first time.

Two years passed, and still the cardinals had not chosen a Pope. The brothers feared that the Khan would think they had forgotten him, so they decided to return to his court without waiting any longer.
In 1271 Marco was seventeen when he left Venice with his father and his uncle. He could not know that he would not see his home again for twenty-four years.
The Polos sailed to Acre and went again to see Teobaldo, the church leader. He wrote letters to the Khan to explain that no Pope had yet been chosen, and he wished them a safe journey.

The Polos then travelled to Jerusalem, where they received a little oil from the lamp at the tomb of Jesus. They carried it carefully, because it was a gift for Kublai Khan, who had asked for it three years before.
The Polos had reached the port of Ayas when a messenger caught up with them. Teobaldo had been elected Pope, he said, and wanted to see them again before they travelled any further.

Back at Acre, the new Pope Gregory gave the brothers letters for the Khan and sent two friars to go with them. These men were meant to teach Christian ideas at the Khan's court, as the Khan had asked.
Near Ayas the sultan of Egypt, Baibars, was raiding the region, and fighting could be heard not far away. The two friars lost heart and turned back, so the three Polos continued on their own.
The Polos next crossed the country we call Turkey, where Marco noticed some of the finest and loveliest carpets in the world. He also saw that the local people wove silk cloth in many colours.
The way then climbed into the high country of Armenia, where the winters are long and the snow lies deep. The Polos wore thick coats, and they kept their horses close to the road.
Marco saw a very high mountain in Armenia and wrote that Noah's ark rests on its top. He says the snow never melts there, so nobody can climb to the summit.
In Georgia the Polos came to a narrow pass between steep mountains and the Caspian Sea. Marco was told that Alexander the Great had once closed it with an iron gate to keep out enemies.
At Baku there was a spring of oil that flowed so strongly that many ships could be filled at once. It was not good to eat, but people burned it in lamps and rubbed it on camels that had itchy skin.
The Polos then came to Mosul, a large town on the Tigris river. The cloth that we call muslin takes its name from Mosul, and merchants from all over the region came there to buy it.

The Polos then came to Baghdad, which for centuries had been the home of the caliph, the chief ruler of the Muslim world. The Mongols had taken the city in 1258, about thirteen years before Marco passed through it.
Marco tells a story he heard in Baghdad about a caliph who challenged the Christians to move a mountain by prayer. A poor cobbler with one eye prayed, and the people said the mountain moved.

Tabriz, in the north of Persia, was a bustling market where merchants from India, Europe and China bought and sold. The city made fine silk and gold cloth, and Marco thought it was a good place to make money.
Marco watched the traders of Tabriz as they weighed pearls and counted coins. He had been taught to trade in Venice, but here he saw prices and customs that no Venetian had ever seen.
Persia was famous for its horses, and Marco says that merchants sold many of them in India. Because Indian horses were weak, buyers there paid very high prices for the strong Persian ones.
Travellers in Persia often stopped at night at large inns with high walls, where camels and horses could be kept safe. Merchants shared food and news, and Marco learned a lot from them.
Whenever the Polos showed the Khan's golden tablet, officials bowed and gave them whatever they asked. They received horses, food and guides, and the Mongol soldiers on the road left them alone.
At Saveh, a town in Persia, Marco was shown three tombs. The people there said the Three Wise Men of the Christmas story were buried in them, side by side in fine tombs.
In Saveh, Marco heard a story about the Wise Men's journey. The baby gave them a small closed box, and when they opened it, they found a stone that became a fire.
The Polos next travelled through Yazd, a good city on the edge of a great desert. The people there wove a silk cloth that merchants carried to many other lands.

On this road, groups of raiders called Caraunas often attacked caravans and took everything the travellers owned. Marco says he was nearly caught once, but he escaped to a village and so did not lose his life.

In Kerman the Polos saw mines that produced turquoise, a bright blue-green stone. The people there also made fine weapons, saddles and embroidered cloth, and the Khan's Mongol soldiers bought a great deal of it.
From Kerman the road went down to a low and very hot plain close to the sea. Marco says the heat there was so strong that a hot wind could be dangerous in summer.

At last the Polos reached the port of Hormuz, where ships arrived from India with pearls, spices, cloth and precious stones. Marco says the town was very rich, but the heat was almost too much to bear.
The Polos looked closely at the ships of Hormuz. They were sewn together with coconut fibre instead of iron nails, and Marco thought they were far too dangerous.
The Polos turned north again and crossed a long desert, where there was almost no water. What little they found was bitter and salty, and they had to carry their own supplies.

Marco heard a tale about the Old Man of the Mountain, a leader who lived in a castle in northern Persia. The story says that he kept a secret garden to make his young followers loyal, though historians doubt much of it.
In what is now Afghanistan the Polos passed through Balkh. Marco says it had once been a noble city, but the Mongols had destroyed many of its fine buildings.
In Badakhshan, Marco fell so ill that the Polos could not go on. He says that the clean mountain air cured him, but it took nearly a year before he was strong enough to travel.

Badakhshan was famous for its rubies, and its mountains also held the deep blue stone called lapis lazuli. Marco says the king kept the best stones for himself and did not let anyone sell them freely.
From Badakhshan the Polos followed a river valley that climbed higher and higher. Ahead of them lay the Pamir, one of the highest mountain regions in the world.
Marco noticed that no birds flew over the high Pamir plateau. He also says that fire burned less brightly there and did not cook food as well, which is true, because of the thin, cold air.
Marco saw wild sheep on the high plateau with huge horns, some six palms long. Today scientists call this animal Marco Polo's sheep in his honour.
Marco says it took the Polos twelve days to cross the Pamir, and for the whole time they found no houses and no grass. They carried all their food and everything else they needed.
When the Polos came down from the mountains, they found Kashgar, a town with gardens, vineyards and cotton fields. Marco says that many of its merchants travelled to far countries to trade.
The road then led to Yarkand, a town on a river. Marco noticed that many people there had swollen throats, which he blamed on the local water, though we cannot be sure he was right.
Khotan was famous for jade, a hard green and white stone. People searched the river beds for pieces, and merchants carried the finest ones to China, where craftsmen valued them highly.
East of Khotan, the Polos passed through small towns at the edge of a vast desert. The rivers that flowed down from the mountains disappeared into the sand, and the green land ended suddenly.
At Lop, a town at the edge of the desert, the Polos rested for about a week. They bought enough food for a month, because they would not find a single village on the other side.
Marco says the desert was so wide that it took about a month to cross it at its narrowest point. There was drinking water at some stops, but it was often bitter and there was never much of it.
Marco says that travellers who fall behind the group may hear voices calling their names. They believe their friends are speaking, so they follow the sound and are never seen again.
He adds that travellers heard strange music in the desert, especially the sound of drums, and believed that spirits made it. The people of the caravan said these spirits wanted to lead them astray.
The Polos left the desert at Dunhuang, called Sachiu in Marco's book. He saw a funeral custom in which people burned paper horses, servants and money for the dead to use in the next life.
In the temples of the region Marco met Buddhist monks, whom he called idol worshippers. He wrote down what he heard about Buddha, although he did not understand the religion well.

Ganzhou, which Marco calls Campichu, was a large city where Christians, Muslims and Buddhists lived together. He says the Polos stayed there for about a year, probably to trade and to wait for news from the Khan.
In Ganzhou Marco saw huge statues lying down in the temples, covered in gold, with many smaller ones standing around them. A big sleeping Buddha built there in 1098 can still be seen.
The Khan heard that the Polos were close and sent messengers to meet them, forty days' ride from his court. They carried fresh horses and food, and they rode with the Polos all the way.
In about 1275 the Polos reached Shangdu, the summer capital of the Khan. A white marble palace stood there on a high, green plain, far north of Khanbaliq.
Marco says a wall about sixteen miles long enclosed the park of Shangdu. Inside were meadows, streams and woods, with deer and other animals that the Khan loved to hunt.
In the park stood a second palace made of bamboo cane, covered with gold and bright paint. It was held up by more than two hundred silk cords, and it could be taken down and moved.
The brothers bowed low before Kublai, who welcomed them like old friends. Then Niccolò presented his son Marco, and the Khan said that the young man was welcome too.
The Polos handed over the letters from Teobaldo and the flask of holy oil from Jerusalem. The Khan accepted them with great respect and ordered that the oil be kept carefully.
The Khan held a feast in honour of the travellers, with many lords and ladies sitting at long tables. Marco says that for days afterwards the people of the court talked about nothing else.
Marco was quick and clever, and soon he spoke four languages and could write four scripts. He did not want only to look around; he wanted to understand the court he was living in.
The Khan decided to test the young man and sent him on a mission to a far land. Marco paid close attention to everything he saw, because he wanted to have something to say when he came home.

When Marco returned, he told the Khan about his business and also about everything he had seen. He described the customs of the people, their food and their strange stories, and the Khan listened with delight.
From then on the Khan trusted Marco and sent him on many missions across the empire. Marco says he served the Khan for about seventeen years, and everything he saw went into his notes.
When the cold came, the Khan and his court moved south to Khanbaliq, the city that Kublai had built. It stood beside an older town, and Marco says the Khan had moved the old people into the new city.
Marco says the city was a perfect square, with walls about six miles long on each side. There were twelve gates, three on every side, and each had its own guards.
The streets of Khanbaliq were so straight that a man could stand at one gate and see all the way to the other. Beside them stood fine houses, each with its own courtyard and garden.
In the middle of the city stood a tower with a great bell. After it rang at night, nobody was allowed in the street, unless he was a doctor or had some other urgent reason.
The palace stood inside many walls and gates, with a marble stair leading up to a huge hall. Marco says six thousand people could sit down to eat in it at one time.
The roof of the palace shone in many colours, with tiles of red, green, blue and yellow. Marco says they were so smooth and bright that they sparkled in the sun and could be seen from far away.
Beside the palace stood a high hill built by hand from earth. The Khan filled it with evergreen trees, so it stayed green all year and is called the Green Mound.
The palace park held a lake with fish for the Khan's table and a stone bridge across it. Beside it were meadows with deer and other tame animals, and white deer that the Khan liked best.

Khanbaliq was a city of trade, and merchants came there from all over the world. Marco says that a thousand carts loaded with silk arrived there every day, which shows how much the city bought and sold.
The Khan kept astrologers who studied the stars and gave him advice. Marco says there were about five thousand of them, and they came from Christian, Muslim and Chinese families.
In Khanbaliq Marco visited the Khan's mint, where money was made from paper. The paper came from the inner bark of the mulberry tree, the same tree whose leaves feed silkworms.
The paper was cut into rectangles of different sizes, each worth a different amount. Officials signed each note, and the master of the mint stamped it with the Khan's red seal.
Whenever merchants brought gold, pearls or precious stones to the Khan, he paid for them with paper notes. The merchants took the notes happily, because they could spend them anywhere in the empire.
Everybody in the empire had to accept the Khan's notes as real money. Marco says a person who refused them could be punished, but most people were happy to use them.
When a note became old or torn, its owner could take it to the mint. There he could exchange it for a new one by paying a small fee.
Marco noticed that the people of Khanbaliq burned black stones that were dug out of the mountains. The stones burned like logs, and they made a hot fire that lasted all night.
The people of Khanbaliq used the black stones to heat their baths, and Marco says that they washed several times a week. In Europe, at that time, people bathed much less often.
Marco was fascinated by the Khan's system of messengers and post stations. On every main road there were post houses about twenty-five miles apart, where messengers could rest and take a fresh horse.
The messengers wore belts hung with little bells, so that the next station could hear them coming. In this way, Marco says, a rider could cover two hundred miles in a single day.
The Khan ordered that trees be planted along the main roads, so that travellers would have shade and could see the road in snow. He also kept great stores of grain for years when the harvest was bad.
The Khan's birthday fell in late September, and it was a day of great celebration. Marco says that the lords of the court all wore robes of the same colour that the Khan had given them.
The great feast of the year came in February, at the New Year, and everyone wore white. People believed that white clothes brought luck for the coming year.
The people brought gifts of gold, silk and white horses to the Khan. Then a parade of elephants and camels, covered with rich cloths, passed in front of the palace.
The Khan sat at a table on a high platform, and his family sat near him. The other guests sat at lower tables, in order of their rank, so that the Khan could see everyone.
The servants who brought the Khan his food and drink covered their noses and mouths with silk cloths. In this way, their breath could not touch what the Khan ate.
Marco admired the Khan's soldiers, who could ride for ten days without cooking any food. They drank mare's milk and carried dried milk paste in small bags, which they mixed with water.

The Khan kept a great herd of pure white mares, and only his family and a few people could drink their milk. Each year he poured some milk on the ground, so that the spirits would protect his animals.
Every spring the Khan went hunting, and thousands of falconers, huntsmen and dogs rode with him. Marco says that the sight of so many men and birds out in the open was very beautiful.
The Khan did not ride a horse on these trips. He was carried in a wooden room, lined with gold cloth, which stood on the backs of four elephants.
The Khan's hunting camp looked like a city of tents. His own tent was so big, Marco says, that a thousand knights could stand inside it, and its walls were hung with tiger skins.
Over the years the Khan sent Marco to far parts of the empire. He rode with the Khan's tablet and kept notes of what he saw, so that he could report it later.
In the city of Taiyuan, Marco found vineyards, which were rare in that part of China. The wine was sold all over the region, and the city's workshops also made iron tools and weapons.
Near Khanbaliq, Marco crossed a famous stone bridge that he calls Pulisanghin. It had many arches and marble pillars, each with a carved lion, and it was one of the finest bridges he knew.
Marco came next to the great city of Xi'an, which was famous for silk and for its busy trade. A Mongol prince, one of the Khan's sons, lived in a fine palace there.
From Xi'an the road climbed through high mountains and deep valleys into Sichuan. In Chengdu, Marco found a long wooden bridge with a roof and with shops built along both sides.
In the south-west, Marco saw how travellers made fires from green bamboo. The canes burst with a loud bang that could be heard from far away, and horses that were new to it ran off in fear.
On the edge of Tibet, Marco learned about a small deer whose scent is used to make perfume. He also saw that some people there used little cakes of salt as money.
In Yunnan Marco found huge creatures that he calls great serpents, with two short legs and enormous jaws. They were crocodiles, and the local people hunted them for their skins and their meat.
Marco noticed that the people of one town covered their teeth with thin caps of gold. They also paid for things with small white shells called cowries, instead of coins.
In 1277 the Khan's army met the king of Burma, who had hundreds of elephants carrying wooden towers. The Mongols tied their frightened horses to trees and shot arrows until the elephants ran away.
The south of China was ruled by the Song, and Marco calls it Mangi. It was richer and more crowded than the north, and Kublai Khan wanted to add it to his empire.
The strong city of Xiangyang stood on a river with high walls and deep water around it. It resisted the Mongol army for about five years, and the Khan's generals could not take it.

In his book, Marco says that the Polos helped to make great machines that threw huge stones. However, the siege ended in 1273, before Marco arrived, and Chinese records give the credit to engineers from Persia.
The Khan chose a general named Bayan to lead his armies south. Marco says the name means Hundred Eyes in Chinese, because the general saw everything, though this is probably a mistake.
Marco was amazed by the great river Yangtze, which in places was so wide that it looked like a sea. He says more ships sailed on it than on all the rivers and seas of Europe.
In 1276 the Song capital of Hangzhou surrendered to the Mongols. The emperor was only a small child, and the army treated the city gently, so it was not burned or ruined.
Marco says that the Khan made him governor of Yangzhou for three years. No Chinese record mentions his name, so perhaps he held a smaller job there.
Near Yangzhou, Marco learned how salt was made along the coast, and how heavily the Khan taxed it. He says the tax on salt was one of the Khan's greatest sources of money.
Marco saw the great canal that joined the Yangtze region to the north. Parts of it were very old, and the Khan's engineers had added new stretches so that barges could reach the capital.
At the canal towns, boats loaded with rice, salt and silk passed in long lines. There were so many that nobody could count them, and Marco must have thought of the boats of Venice.
Marco came at last to Hangzhou, which he calls Quinsai, a name that he says means City of Heaven. He believed it was the finest and noblest city in the world.
Marco says that the city wall was about a hundred miles round, though it may have been less. On one side lay a great lake, and on the other side flowed a wide river.
