Marco says that Hangzhou had twelve thousand stone bridges. The arches of the main ones were so high that a ship could sail under them without lowering its mast.
In the city, Marco counted ten large market squares. People came from the whole region to buy fish, meat, fruit, vegetables and spices, and nearby stood large stone warehouses.
The streets of Hangzhou were paved with stone and brick, which made them clean and easy to walk on. Marco says that there were twelve main trades, each with twelve thousand workshops.
Marco noticed that every house had a small board by the door. It listed the people who lived there, and innkeepers wrote down the name and arrival day of each guest.
On the west side of the city lay the great lake, which Marco says was about thirty miles round. Its shores were crowded with temples, gardens and the homes of rich families.
On the lake, people could hire large pleasure boats with painted cabins and silk awnings. Marco says they held feasts on the water and enjoyed the fine view of the city.
Marco visited the old palace of the Song kings, which stood in a walled enclosure. It held many halls, painted rooms and gardens, and the Khan's governor kept it in good order.
Marco says that guards stood on every bridge and in each street at night. The merchants kept their goods in stone towers, because wooden houses often burned in fires.
From Hangzhou the road led south through green hills, rivers and many busy towns. Marco crossed into Fujian, where the land was covered with forests and bamboo.
In Fuzhou Marco found ginger and other spices at very low prices. He also saw sugar being made, and he heard that people from Egypt had taught the local people how to refine it.
In the town of Tingiu, now called Dehua, Marco saw workshops that made fine white bowls and dishes. They were so cheap, he says, that a Venetian coin would buy three of them.
At last Marco reached Zaiton, which is now called Quanzhou. He says that it was one of the two greatest ports in the world, with ships arriving from India and the islands.
Marco says that for every ship of pepper that went to Egypt for Europe, a hundred came to Zaiton. The Khan took a large share of every cargo as a tax.
Merchants from India, Persia, Arabia and other places lived in Zaiton, and the city was full of temples and mosques. Marco liked the way so many peoples shared one city.
Marco describes the great ships of China, which were much bigger than any he knew. They were made of fir wood, with two layers of planks and four masts.
The hull of each ship was divided into thirteen sections by strong walls. If a leak started in one part, the water could not pass to the others, so the ship stayed afloat.
A big ship could carry three hundred sailors and many passengers, with small boats hanging at its sides. Marco says the crew even grew vegetables in wooden tubs on the deck.
In Zaiton, Marco heard about Japan, which he calls Cipangu, an island far out in the eastern sea. He was told that its king had a palace roofed with pure gold, though Marco never went there.
Marco tells how the Khan sent two fleets against Japan, in 1274 and 1281. Storms wrecked many of the ships, and only a few of the soldiers came home.
The Polos had been in China for many years, and they had become rich. They wanted to go home, but they were afraid of what might happen after the old Khan died.
When Niccolò asked the Khan for permission to leave, the old ruler said no. He was fond of the Polos, and he could not understand why anyone would want to leave his rich court.
Then three messengers arrived from Arghun, the Mongol ruler of Persia. His wife had died, and before her death she had asked that her successor should come from her own family.
The Khan chose a girl of seventeen called Kokachin, who was beautiful and clever and belonged to the right family. The envoys were delighted with her, and they agreed to take her to Persia.
War had closed the land road to Persia, so the envoys wanted to go by ship. Marco had just come back from a voyage to India, and they asked the Khan to let the Polos guide them.
At last the Khan agreed, though he was sad to lose them. He gave the Polos golden tablets that would protect them, and also letters to the Pope and to several kings of Europe.
The Khan ordered fourteen ships to be made ready, each with four masts. Marco says they carried about six hundred passengers, apart from the sailors, and food for two years.
In about 1291 the fleet left Zaiton and sailed out onto the open sea. Marco, his father and his uncle stood on the deck and watched China slowly disappear behind them.
After about three months at sea, the fleet reached Champa, in what is now Vietnam. Marco says that its king paid the Khan a yearly gift of elephants, since the Mongols had once defeated him.
The fleet sailed past Java, which sailors said was the richest island of all. Marco did not land there, and he writes only what the sailors told him about its pepper, cloves and nutmeg.
At last the fleet arrived at Sumatra, but the winds were against them. They had to wait for about five months for the monsoon to change before they could sail on.
To stay safe during the long wait, the travellers built a wooden fort with a ditch around it. They bought food from the local people and tried palm wine and bread made from the sago tree.
On Sumatra, Marco saw a large animal that he called a unicorn. It had one black horn and loved mud, and it was not the white beauty of the old stories.

In the town of Perlak, Marco found that many people followed the Muslim faith. Merchants from Arabia and Persia had come there to trade, and over the years they had taught their religion to the local people.
In Ceylon, now called Sri Lanka, Marco heard about a ruby as long as a man's hand. The Khan sent messengers to buy it, but the king would not sell it for any price.
In Ceylon Marco heard about a high mountain called Adam's Peak. Pilgrims climbed it with the help of iron chains, and at the top they found a footprint in the rock.
Off the coast of southern India, merchants hired divers to collect pearl oysters from the sea bottom. The divers held their breath, and some men said that spells kept sharks away from them.
In Mylapore, on the south-east coast of India, Marco found a small church. He was told that it held the tomb of Saint Thomas the Apostle, and that both Christians and Muslims came to visit it.
On the Malabar coast, Marco saw gardens of pepper, ginger and cinnamon, and ships came in from all over the east. He also heard that pirates there sailed in large groups and robbed passing ships.
After about two years, the fleet reached Hormuz in Persia. Marco says that of the six hundred passengers, only eighteen were still alive, because sickness had killed the rest.
The travellers learned that Arghun had died while they were at sea. His brother Gaikhatu was now ruling the country, and the Polos asked him what should be done with Kokachin.
Gaikhatu said that the princess should marry Arghun's son, Ghazan, who was about twenty-two. After the wedding, Marco says, Kokachin wept when she said goodbye to the Polos.
The Polos rested for several months in Tabriz, the rich Persian city that they knew well. Gaikhatu gave them golden tablets, which would let them travel safely and find help on their way home.
From Tabriz the Polos rode across the mountains to Trebizond, a port on the Black Sea. There they found ships and prepared to sail towards Constantinople.
The Polos crossed the Black Sea and came again to Constantinople, where Niccolò and Maffeo had once traded. From there they took ship through the Greek islands towards Venice.
In 1295, after about twenty-four years away, the three Polos arrived in Venice. They looked tired and dusty, and they wore plain, worn clothes that had been made in distant lands.
At the family house, the relatives hardly recognised the travellers. The three men had a foreign look, and they spoke Venetian with a strange accent, since they had not used it for so long.
A famous story says that the Polos held a feast and showed their old coats. They cut open the linings, and a stream of jewels poured out, so that everyone believed them at last.

People in Venice began to call Marco Il Milione, which means The Million. Nobody is sure why, but maybe it was because of his wealth or his many stories, and a courtyard in Venice still carries the name.
Venice and Genoa were the two great sea powers of Italy, and they were bitter rivals. In the 1290s their rivalry turned into open war, and Venice called on its citizens to fight.
According to an old tradition, Marco paid for a war galley and sailed with the fleet. The records are not clear, but it is likely that he took part in the fight in some way.
In September 1298 the two fleets met off the island of Curzola, in the Adriatic Sea. The Genoese, led by Lamba Doria, won a great victory and took thousands of Venetians prisoner.
Marco was taken to Genoa as a prisoner, along with many other Venetians. He had to wait there while the two cities argued about the terms of peace, and the wait could last for months.
In the prison Marco met Rustichello of Pisa, who had been captured in an earlier sea battle, at Meloria in 1284. Rustichello was a writer of romances, which were popular stories about knights.
Marco told his stories aloud, day after day, and Rustichello wrote them down on paper. A tradition says that Marco sent to Venice for his notes, which would have helped him remember small details.
The book was written in French, then the language of travel stories. Its first words call on emperors, kings, knights and everyone else who wants to learn about the different peoples of the world.
The book describes cities, roads, customs, goods and animals, one place after another. Marco usually says plainly when he saw something himself and when he only heard about it from other people.
In 1299 Genoa and Venice made peace, and the Venetian prisoners were released. Marco went home to Venice, where he would spend the rest of his life, and Rustichello returned to Pisa.
Back in Venice, Marco married Donata Badoer, and they had three daughters, called Fantina, Bellela and Moreta. He lived quietly as a merchant, in a house near the church of San Giovanni Crisostomo.

There were no printing presses in Europe yet, so the book spread when scribes copied it by hand. Soon there were versions in French, Latin, Italian and other languages, and about a hundred and fifty of them still exist.
Some readers believed every word, and some thought that Marco was telling tall tales. The huge numbers in his stories made the doubters laugh, and they called him Il Milione.
Modern critics have asked why Marco says nothing about tea or the Great Wall. They find it strange that a man who lived in China for seventeen years would leave these things out.

Others point out that the stone Great Wall we know was built later. Marco also used Persian names for places, because Persian was spoken at court, and his details of paper money, coal and the post are correct.
In January 1324 Marco, now about seventy, made his will. He left money to his wife and daughters, and he freed his servant Peter, who had come with him from the East.
A famous story says that friends asked the dying Marco to take back his stories. He answered that he had not told even half of what he had seen.
In the 1450s Fra Mauro, a Venetian monk, drew a huge round map of the world. He took many names of cities and lands in Asia from the book of Marco Polo.
Christopher Columbus owned a printed copy of Marco's book and wrote many notes in the margins. He wanted to reach the lands of the Great Khan by sailing west across the sea.

Over the next centuries, many travellers went east, with Marco's book in their bags. Around 1600, Jesuit missionaries and travellers finally proved that Cathay, in the book, was the same land as China.
Today the Travels of Marco Polo is read in many languages all around the world. The airport of Venice carries his name, and a small courtyard in the city still reminds visitors of Il Milione.
C1C2: In the thirteenth century, Venice was one of the richest trading cities in Europe, a place of canals and marble churches where ships arrived daily loaded with spices, silk and gossip from distant shores. Into this world Marco Polo was born around 1254, the son of a merchant family whose men were used to travelling for years at a time. His father, Niccolò, and his uncle Maffeo were already far away on a journey, and the boy grew up without once seeing the man whose name he bore.

Venice had been built on muddy islands in a shallow lagoon, yet by Marco's childhood it had grown into a great power of the sea, with a fleet that carried its flag from Constantinople to Egypt. Its wealth rested on trade, and every merchant family dreamed of reaching the lands where silk and spices began their journeys. A boy raised in such a place learned early that the world was large, and that fortunes were made at its far edges.

In Constantinople the two brothers had prospered, selling goods to buyers from every corner of the known world. Around 1260, being merchants who never let an opportunity pass, they turned most of their profit into jewels, which are easy to carry and valuable everywhere. Then they set out towards the unknown lands beyond the Black Sea, with no idea how long they would be gone.

After crossing the Black Sea to Soldaia, in the Crimea, the brothers joined a caravan and rode for many days over a sea of grass that seemed to have no end. At its edge, beside the great river Volga, stood the camp of Berke, a Mongol ruler and a grandson of the famous conqueror Genghis Khan. It was a world of felt tents, herds of horses and riders who had never seen a Venetian.

Berke received the strangers with courtesy, and he was so taken with their jewels that he paid them much more than they had hoped, in gifts as well as in coin. The brothers remained at his camp for about a year, learning something of the Mongol language and the manners of the court. It was a useful lesson for two men who would soon need to deal with a far greater ruler.

Their stay ended abruptly when war broke out between Berke and Hulagu, another grandson of Genghis Khan, and armies cut the road by which they had come. Unable to go home, the brothers decided to go forward instead, and they travelled east across a bare desert that took them seventeen days to cross. At the end of it lay Bukhara, a rich city of merchants and scholars in the heart of Central Asia.

For three long years the brothers lived in Bukhara, a city of domes and markets, hoping that the fighting would end and the roads would reopen. They were not idle, since men like them could always find a profit, and they must have used the time to study the customs of the people around them. Yet the way to Venice stayed closed, and every month they grew a little further from the world they knew.

One day envoys sent by Hulagu arrived in Bukhara on their way to the court of Kublai, the Great Khan, who ruled the whole of the East. Surprised to find two Europeans there, they said that their master had never in his life met a man from the Latin lands and would be delighted to receive them. The brothers considered it carefully, and they decided that a road to the Khan was better than no road at all.

The journey to the Khan's court took a full year, for snow, swollen rivers and rough country forced the party to halt again and again. Along the way the brothers saw marvels enough to fill a book, though it was Marco, years later, who would be the one to write about the East. For now they simply rode on, northwards and eastwards, towards a ruler greater than any they had met.

At last the two Venetians were led into the presence of Kublai, the grandson of Genghis Khan and the most powerful ruler on Earth. Instead of the cold greeting they might have feared, he welcomed them warmly, glad of strangers who could tell him of a world he had only heard about. The brothers had come to the end of one great journey, and they could not yet guess that it was only the first.

Kublai was curious about everything, and he questioned the brothers for hours about the emperors and kings of Europe, their laws, their wars and the way they kept order among their people. Because they had picked up the Mongol language during their long journey, they were able to answer him directly, without an interpreter. The Khan listened closely, and he seemed to be pleased with everything he heard.

The Khan's questions turned next to the Pope, the leader of the Christian church, and to the beliefs that guided the lives of Europeans. His own empire held Buddhists, Muslims and Christians among its peoples, and he was curious to find out whether this faith had something worth learning. The brothers answered as well as they could, and what they said made a strong impression on him.

After several long conversations, Kublai made up his mind to use the brothers as his messengers to the West, since they knew both worlds and he trusted them. He chose a Mongol noble named Cogatal to travel with them and to give their mission the weight of his own authority. It was a very great honour for two merchants from Venice, and it would change the course of their lives.

The Khan's letter asked the Pope to send him a hundred wise men, each skilled in the sciences and the arts of Europe, who could explain the Christian faith to his scholars. If they could prove that their religion was better than the others in his empire, he promised, he and his people would consider adopting it. It was an extraordinary invitation, and the history of Asia and Europe might have been different if it had been fully answered.

Kublai added one more request, which was for a small quantity of oil from the lamp that burns above the tomb of Jesus in Jerusalem, a place of deep reverence for Christians. He had been told of its holiness by the Christians at his court, and he valued it as a gift from the very centre of their faith. The brothers promised to bring it, and nobody who knew their determination doubted that they would do their very best.

Before they set out, Kublai gave the brothers a golden tablet inscribed with his command, which acted as a kind of passport across the whole of his empire. Whoever saw it was obliged to supply them with horses, food, shelter and an escort, and no one dared to harm those who carried it. In the years that followed, that small piece of gold would carry them across thousands of miles.

They had not gone far before Cogatal fell seriously ill, and it became clear that he could not complete the journey. The brothers left him to recover in a nearby town, and they went on without him, trusting in the Khan's golden tablet to open every door. Everywhere they stopped, officials bowed to the tablet and gave them everything they needed.

Bad weather made the return journey much slower than the outward one, for snow blocked the passes and spring floods drowned the roads for weeks at a time. It was nearly three years before they reached the port of Ayas, on the coast of Armenia, and from there they took ship to Acre, arriving in April 1269. They had been away from the Christian world for so long that Europe now seemed almost as foreign as Asia.

At Acre the brothers received unwelcome news, for Pope Clement had died the year before, and the cardinals had not yet agreed on a successor. A respected church leader named Teobaldo, who lived in the city, advised them to wait until a new Pope was chosen and then deliver the Khan's letter to him. There was nothing to be done but to go home to Venice and wait, which they were glad to do after such a long absence.

When the brothers finally reached Venice, Niccolò learned that his wife had died during his long absence, and that the son he had left unborn was now a boy of about fifteen. Father and son met for the first time that day, and we can only imagine what they said to each other. For Marco, the weathered stranger in the doorway had brought with him a world he was about to join.

Two years passed in Venice, and still the cardinals could not agree on a new Pope, leaving the Khan's letter with no one to receive it. The brothers feared that Kublai would believe they had broken their word, and they judged it wiser to go back and explain than to wait indefinitely. This time they decided that Niccolò's son, who was now almost a man, would travel with them.

In 1271 the three Polos boarded a ship in Venice, and the seventeen-year-old Marco watched the towers of his native city sink slowly into the lagoon. He had been waiting all his life to join the adventures of his father and uncle, yet he could hardly have imagined how long this one would last. He did not know that it would be twenty-four long years before he saw that lagoon again.

After a sea voyage along the Mediterranean, the Polos landed at Acre and went at once to see Teobaldo, the church leader who had advised them earlier. Since there was still no Pope, he wrote letters to Kublai explaining the delay and confirming that the brothers had done everything they could to carry out the Khan's wishes. Armed with this proof of their good faith, they prepared for the long road ahead.

From Acre the Polos rode to Jerusalem, where they fulfilled the Khan's second request by filling a small flask with oil from the lamp that burns above the tomb of Jesus. They carried it with great care, for it was both a holy object and a promise that they had made three years earlier. Marco himself was seeing the Holy Land for the first time, and it must have been an unforgettable moment for a young traveller.

The Polos had barely reached the port of Ayas when a messenger arrived with astonishing news, for the cardinals had at last made their choice, and it was Teobaldo himself. He had taken the name Gregory, and as Pope he wished to speak with the brothers again before they went on. Turning around so soon was a nuisance, but they could hardly refuse the head of the church.

At Acre the new Pope received the Venetians with honour and entrusted them with letters for the Khan, together with two learned friars, Nicholas and William, to represent the church at Kublai's court. He could not provide the hundred wise men the Khan had requested, but he offered what he had, with his blessing. Once again the travellers turned back towards Ayas, now a company of five, with the Pope's blessing and a fresh supply of hope.

Soon after they left, the sultan of Egypt, Baibars, began a wave of raids in the region, and the news of war frightened the two friars so badly that they decided to turn back. They handed their letters to the Polos and returned to safety, abandoning the mission after only a few days. The three Venetians, who were more used to danger, shrugged off the setback and went forward alone.

Heading north and east through the land that is now Turkey, the travellers passed through towns where the markets glowed with colour. Marco later praised the carpets made there as the finest and most beautiful in the world, and he noted that the same people produced silk of every shade. A merchant by blood and training, he must have wondered how much they would fetch in Venice.

From Turkey the road climbed into the rough highlands of Armenia, where the winters are long, the winds are bitter and the snow can lie for months. The Polos pulled their thick coats around them, hired local guides and made slow progress past Erzurum, where the road grew steeper with every day. Even so, they pressed on day after day, because they knew that the Great Khan was waiting for them at the end of the road.

Marco gazed up at a huge mountain, whose peak was hidden under snow that never melts, and was told that Noah's ark had come to rest on its summit after the Flood. He says that the snow lies so deep and so constantly that no one can reach the top, which may explain why the tale has lasted so long. Whether or not the story is true, the huge snowy mountain remains one of the most striking sights on the whole road to the East.

Beyond Armenia lay Georgia, and there the road squeezed through a narrow strip of land between steep mountains and the shore of the Caspian Sea. Marco was told that Alexander the Great had once shut this pass with an iron gate to keep out the wild tribes of the north, a story that has been repeated in that region for centuries. Whether or not the gate ever existed, the pass was certainly an ideal place to stop an army.

Near Baku, Marco saw a spring from which black oil poured in such quantities that a hundred ships could be loaded at once. Nobody could eat it, but the local people burned it in their lamps and used it as a medicine for camels that suffered from skin disease. In the next centuries this same ground would become one of the most famous oilfields in the world, though Marco could not have known that.

Further south, the road led the Polos to Mosul, a large and busy city on the banks of the Tigris river. The fine cotton cloth that we still call muslin is named after this place, and Marco notes that merchants arrived there from many countries to buy it by the bale. It is one of the few words in modern English that preserve the memory of a town on Marco's road.

Next they reached Baghdad, the great city on the Tigris that had been the capital of the caliphs, the spiritual rulers of the Muslim world, for more than five hundred years. In 1258 a Mongol army led by Hulagu had captured it, ending the caliphate there, and the city was still recovering when Marco arrived about thirteen years later. Even in decline it was a place of famous markets, scholars and buildings, and it left a deep impression on the young traveller.

In Baghdad Marco heard a famous tale about a caliph who challenged the Christians of his city to prove their faith by moving a mountain through prayer. According to the story, a humble cobbler with one eye knelt and prayed, and the whole mountain shook and shifted before the astonished crowd. Marco, like the people who told it, presents this as a miracle rather than a historical fact, and it is best read as a story.

Tabriz, in the north of Persia, was a bustling market where merchants from India, Arabia and Europe haggled over silks, pearls and precious stones. Marco, who had been trained in the arts of trade since boyhood, studied the traders closely and noted what each of them valued. In his book he calls it a city so well placed that any merchant who lived there could grow rich.

In the bazaars of Tabriz, Marco spent hours watching the traders weigh pearls, test gold and bargain in half a dozen languages. Although he had been taught the basics of commerce at home, he now saw prices and customs that no Venetian had ever recorded. He stored all of it in his memory, and a good deal of it would eventually find its way into his book.

Persia was famous for the quality of its horses, and Marco reports that dealers carried large numbers of them down to the ports and sold them to buyers in India. Since the horses bred in India were thought to be weak, the strong Persian animals commanded very high prices, which made the trade extremely profitable. A Venetian merchant could appreciate such a business, even if he did not own a single horse.

Along the main roads of Persia stood large inns, built of stone around an open courtyard, where caravans could rest at night in safety and shelter. Merchants, soldiers and pilgrims sat around the same fires, trading news, advice and stories about the dangers and the profits ahead. For a curious young man such evenings were as instructive as any lesson, and Marco missed very little.

Whenever the Polos showed the Khan's golden tablet, local officials bowed low and hurried to provide fresh horses, food and trustworthy guides. The Mongol soldiers who patrolled the roads treated the three Venetians as friends of the Khan himself, and that was a protection more valuable than a hundred swords. It made the long journey far safer and far quicker than it would otherwise have been for three foreign merchants.

At Saveh, a Persian town of stone houses and busy markets, Marco was taken to see three handsome tombs standing side by side. The townspeople told him that these were the graves of the Three Wise Men, or Magi, who had travelled to Bethlehem to honour the newborn Jesus. Marco says he was shown the bodies, still with their hair and beards, though he adds that nobody could tell him anything more about them.

The people of Saveh told Marco a curious story about the Wise Men's journey home from Bethlehem, in which the child gave them a small closed box as a gift. When they grew curious and opened it, they found only a stone, which they threw into a well, and a bright fire came down from heaven and burned there. Marco repeats this as something he heard, and he does not claim that it actually happened.

From Saveh the road led towards Yazd, a prosperous city on the edge of a vast desert, whose people were famous for the silk cloth they wove. Merchants carried it over the mountains and across the sea, so that a piece made in a Persian workshop might end up in Venice or in China. Marco, who could recognise a good trade when he saw one, took careful note.

The roads of southern Persia were haunted by bands of raiders called Caraunas, who swept down on caravans, took everything they could carry and sometimes carried off the travellers themselves. Marco says that he was once very nearly caught, though he managed to reach a village in time and so escaped. It was a vivid reminder that even the Khan's golden tablet could not protect a traveller everywhere.

At Kerman, the Polos found a city rich in minerals, for the mountains nearby contained mines of turquoise, the brilliant blue stone prized across Asia. The craftsmen there also made excellent weapons, saddles and embroidery, in which the Mongol officers took great pleasure. Marco listed all of these goods in his book, as a merchant would, with an eye for what could be sold elsewhere.

From Kerman the road descended steeply to a low plain beside the sea, a country so hot that Marco says the people there left their houses in the worst of summer. He adds that a scorching wind sometimes blew in from the sands, which could cause terrible harm to men and animals who were caught in it. The Polos pressed on towards the coast, sweating in the heavy air and hoping that the worst of the heat was behind them.

At last the travellers came to Hormuz, a port where merchants from India landed cargoes of pearls, spices, gems, cloth and elephant tusks. Marco was impressed by the quantity and quality of the goods, though he complained that the heat of the place was so extreme that it was almost impossible to live there. The Polos had hoped to continue the rest of their journey by sea from this port, which would have saved them months.

The Polos took a long, hard look at the ships of Hormuz, and what they saw did not please them. The planks were stitched together with thread made from the fibre of coconuts, without a single iron nail, and Marco says that many of these vessels were lost at sea. Considering the risks very carefully, the three Venetians decided that it would be wiser to go on by land instead.

Turning away from the sea, the Polos struck north across a hard and thirsty desert, where the few springs they found were salty and bitter to the taste. They carried every drop of drinking water they could, and they rationed it carefully, because a mistake here would have been fatal. The desert was a harsh test for a seventeen-year-old, but Marco was learning how to travel.

On the road Marco heard the famous tale of the Old Man of the Mountain, a leader whose castle stood in the mountains of northern Persia. According to the story, he showed his young followers a secret garden full of fountains and fruit, and made them believe it was paradise, so that they would obey him in everything. Historians consider much of this to be legend, and Hulagu's army had already destroyed the real fortress in 1256.

Travelling on through what is now Afghanistan, the Polos reached Balkh, a city that Marco describes as having once been grand and noble. The Mongols had attacked it some fifty years earlier, and many of its palaces and marble buildings lay in ruins, though people still lived among them. It was a sad reminder of what war could do to the great trading cities of the Silk Road.

At Badakhshan, high in the mountains, Marco fell seriously ill, and the travellers had no choice but to stop and wait. He reports that the pure mountain air gradually restored his health, though it was almost a year before he was strong enough to ride again. We do not know what the illness was, but the long delay did not stop him from taking careful notes on everything around him.

Badakhshan was famous for its precious stones, and the mountains yielded rubies, silver and the rich blue stone called lapis lazuli, from which painters made their finest colour. Marco reports that the king claimed the best stones as his own property, and that nobody was allowed to send them out of the kingdom without his permission. He also mentions mountains of salt, a good example of how a merchant sees the world.

Once Marco had recovered, the Polos set out again, following a narrow river valley that climbed steadily towards the Pamir. This is one of the highest regions on the planet, a tangle of snowy ranges that the local people call the roof of the world, and the road across it was rough, steep and lonely. Marco was about to see a landscape quite unlike anything he had ever known in the gentle, watery lands around Venice.

On the high plateau Marco noticed that there were no birds in the sky, a silence that must have felt very strange. He also reports that fire did not burn as brightly or cook food as thoroughly as it did at lower altitudes, which is quite true, since water boils at a lower temperature in thin mountain air. It is one of many accurate observations that make his account so valuable to historians and scientists today.

On the high pastures of the Pamir Marco saw a wild sheep with enormous curling horns, some of them as long as a man's arm, and he says that shepherds made bowls and tools from the horns. Zoologists later named the animal Marco Polo's sheep in his honour, a rare example of a traveller whose name is still on the lips of scientists. He also reports that wolves hunted the sheep in these mountains, and that travellers piled horns and bones beside the track to mark the way when snow fell.

The crossing of the Pamir took twelve days by Marco's count, and in all that time the Polos saw no villages, no inns and no green pasture for their animals. They carried every scrap of food they would need, and slept wherever night found them, wrapped in thick coats against the bitter cold. After the hardships of Persia, it was an even harder test, and the young Marco met it with growing confidence.

Descending from the mountains, the Polos found Kashgar, a green oasis of orchards, vineyards and cotton fields set in the middle of the dry plain. After the hardships of the high plateau the place must have seemed like paradise, and Marco notes that many of the local merchants travelled widely and traded in far countries. The Polos rested here for a while before moving on along the great trade route that later generations called the Silk Road.

From Kashgar the caravan route continued to Yarkand, a prosperous town in a river valley, where Marco paid close attention to the local people. He noticed that many of them suffered from swollen throats and legs, and he blamed the water, though modern doctors might look for other causes. He is careful to say only what he had seen, which is a habit that makes him a trustworthy guide.

At Khotan the Polos came to a town celebrated for its jade, a hard and beautiful stone that was carved into ornaments, bowls and jewellery. Marco learned that the stones were washed down from the mountains and collected from the river beds, and that traders carried the finest pieces all the way to China. The Chinese prized jade above almost anything else, which made it a very profitable cargo.

East of Khotan the road ran along the southern rim of the Taklamakan, a desert so large and empty that the local people feared it. Rivers that rushed down from the mountains simply vanished into the sand, and the green fields ended in a sharp line. The Polos passed through the small towns of Pein and Charchan, buying supplies for the hard weeks ahead.

At Lop, the last town before the great desert, the Polos did what every traveller did, resting a week to recover their strength and gather supplies. They bought enough food for a whole month, loaded it on camels, and filled their leather bags with water, since there was no certainty of finding any more. The people of Lop warned them that the crossing was not to be taken lightly.

By Marco's count the desert took about a month to cross, even at its narrowest, and for most of that time the travellers moved over sand and stone beneath a merciless sun. Water was found only every day or two, in small wells, and what the wells gave was often so bitter that the animals refused to drink. It was one of the hardest stretches of the whole journey, and the Polos moved slowly and carefully through it.

Marco reports that a traveller who lagged behind his companions, or who dozed off in the saddle, might suddenly hear voices calling him by name. Mistaking them for the voices of his friends, he would follow them off the road, and many wanderers were lost in this way, he says, and were never found again. It is a story that many later desert travellers have told, and it probably reflects the effects of thirst, heat and tiredness on the mind.

He adds that the desert also seemed to be full of music, with the sound of drums, pipes and strings drifting across the dunes at night. The caravan people believed that evil spirits made these noises in order to tempt travellers away from the track and into the sand. Modern scientists think that the wind moving over the dunes, along with the strain of the journey, may explain such sounds.

At last the desert ended and the Polos entered Dunhuang, which Marco calls Sachiu, the first town of the Khan's own lands in the East. There he observed a funeral custom that struck him as new: families burned paper models of horses, servants, camels and money, believing that these would serve the dead in the next life. He records it with obvious curiosity, and with none of the scorn that some later European visitors would show for customs that were not their own.

In the towns and temples of this region Marco met Buddhist monks for the first time, and his book calls them worshippers of idols, a label that shows how little he understood their beliefs. Even so, he listened attentively to what he was told about the life of Buddha, and he wrote it down with respect. It was the beginning of a lifelong interest in the many religions of Asia.

Ganzhou, which Marco calls Campichu, was a large and important city in which the three faiths of Christianity, Islam and Buddhism lived side by side, each with its own place of worship. Marco says that the Polos remained there for about a year, probably to do business and to wait for orders from the Khan. It was a good place to see how the Mongols governed so many different peoples.

In Ganzhou's temples Marco saw statues that were far larger than life, some of them lying on their sides and covered with gold leaf, with rows of smaller figures standing round them. A great reclining Buddha, built in the year 1098, still survives in the city today, which matches Marco's description closely. It is exactly the kind of detail that makes his report so believable, and that a man who had never seen the place would have found very hard to invent.

News of the Polos' approach had reached Kublai, and he was so pleased that he sent messengers to meet them, a full forty days' ride from his court. The riders brought fresh horses, rich food and a warm welcome, and from that point onward the Venetians travelled like honoured guests rather than anxious strangers. After nearly four years on the road, the end of the long journey was finally in sight, and the three Venetians must have felt both relief and pride.

After forty days of riding, the Polos came at last to Shangdu, the summer capital of the Great Khan. Its white marble palace rose from a green plain where the summers were cool, far from the heat of the southern cities. The Venetians had crossed half the world to see it, and the sight did not disappoint them.

A wall some sixteen miles round, Marco says, enclosed the great park that lay beside the palace, and within it were fountains, streams, meadows and shady groves. The Khan kept deer and other game there, and he liked to ride out among them with his falcons on his wrist. Marco's description is so lively that the park has been remembered by poets ever since.

Deep in the park, Marco tells us, stood a second palace made of split bamboo, its pillars gilded and its roof coated with varnish to keep out the rain. Over two hundred silk cords held it firmly against the wind, and in autumn the whole building could be taken to pieces and carried away. To a merchant from a city of stone and brick, a palace that could travel was a marvel.

The two brothers knelt before the Khan, who greeted them warmly and asked about their long journey. Niccolò then presented his son Marco, now a young man of about twenty-one, and the Khan said that he was welcome too. It was the first time the boy from Venice had stood before the most powerful ruler on Earth.

The Polos then handed over the letters written by Teobaldo and the little flask of oil they had carried from the tomb in Jerusalem. The Khan received both with evident respect, though he can hardly have understood how holy the oil was to a Christian. He asked who the young man was, and the brothers said that he was Niccolò's son.

To celebrate the safe arrival of his guests, the Khan held a splendid feast at which the chief lords of the court sat down together at long tables. The Polos were seated near the ruler as honoured friends, and they were treated with a kindness they could hardly have dreamed of. For days afterwards the whole court talked of nothing but the strangers from the faraway West, and of the long road that had brought them.

Marco proved to be an unusually gifted student, and within a short time he had learned four languages and the four different scripts in which they were written. His mind was quick and his memory was good, but what set him apart was curiosity, since he wanted to understand the people around him rather than merely to look at them. The Khan, who liked clever people and noticed everything that happened in his court, soon began to watch the young Venetian with interest.

The Khan, wishing to see what the young foreigner could do, gave him a mission to a distant land, and Marco set out with great care. He had noticed that the Khan's other envoys returned with nothing to report but their business, and the Khan found this dull. Marco resolved that he would come back with something more worth hearing, and he began to keep careful notes as he rode.

When Marco returned, he reported on the business of his mission and then went on to describe everything else, including the customs, the foods and the curious stories of the people he had met. The Khan listened with growing delight, for he had never before had an envoy who brought the world home with him. Soon people at court were saying, with a mixture of admiration and envy, that this young foreigner would go very far indeed.

From that day, the Khan relied on Marco and sent him on one mission after another to the farthest corners of the empire. By his own account Marco served the ruler for about seventeen years, and during all that time he watched, listened and remembered. Everything he learned in those years, from the price of pepper to the customs of remote villages, would one day fill a book.

As autumn turned to winter, the court left the cool north and moved to Khanbaliq, the new capital that Kublai had ordered built beside an older town. The Khan had planned the place carefully, and he wanted a city that would show the world how great his empire had become. Marco arrived there with his father and uncle, and he found it more splendid than anything in Europe.

Marco describes Khanbaliq as a perfect square, each of its four sides running to about six miles, with high walls of earth that were white on the outside. Twelve gates pierced the walls, three on each side, and above every gate stood a fine hall where the guards kept their weapons. The plan was so orderly that it seemed to have been drawn with a ruler.

To a Venetian used to bending lanes and crooked canals, the straight streets of Khanbaliq were a wonder in themselves. A man standing at one gate, Marco says, could see clear across the city to the gate at the other end. Along both sides of every street the Khan's people had been given plots of land, on which they built handsome houses with gardens and courtyards.

In the centre of the city a tall tower held a bell so large that its sound carried across the whole of Khanbaliq. Once it had rung in the evening, Marco says, nobody was allowed in the streets, unless a birth or an illness made it necessary, and even then the person had to carry a light. Patrols moved about all night, and anyone found out of doors without good reason was stopped and questioned.

The great palace of the Khan lay inside several walls, and its main hall was so large, Marco says, that six thousand people could sit down to a meal at once. A marble terrace ran all round it, and the walls of the hall were covered with gold and silver and carved dragons. Marco, who had grown up among the palaces of Venice, had never seen anything to compare.

High above, the roof of the palace was covered in tiles of red, green, blue and yellow, so cleverly glazed that they shone like crystal in the sunlight. Marco says that the glitter could be seen from a great distance, and travellers approaching the city would know from afar where the Khan lived. It was the kind of display that was meant to impress, and it certainly impressed him.

Close to the palace the Khan had ordered his workers to build a hill of earth, and he made them cover it with evergreen trees brought from every part of his empire. Where a tree was too large to move easily, Marco says, it was dug up with its roots and carried by elephants. Because the leaves never fell, the hill stayed green in every season, and it came to be called the Green Mound.

Beside the Green Mound lay a lake that was kept full of fish for the Khan's table, and a handsome stone bridge crossed it. The park around it was home to tame deer, goats and other gentle creatures, which the Khan watched with real pleasure as he walked along the paths. It was a place of peace in the middle of a busy capital, and a reminder that even the greatest of rulers needed somewhere quiet to rest.

Merchants and goods flowed into Khanbaliq from every direction, and the suburbs outside the walls were crowded with inns where foreign traders stayed. Marco claims that a thousand cartloads of silk arrived at the gates each day, a figure that is surely exaggerated, but it conveys his sense of the city's wealth. Everything that was rare or precious in the world, he says, could be found in its markets.

The Khan took great interest in the study of the sky, and Marco says that about five thousand astrologers, Christian, Muslim and Chinese, were supported at his court. Each year they prepared a calendar that told people when to plant, when to travel and which days were fortunate for important business. The Khan consulted them before any major decision, and Marco, being a curious man, was glad to learn from them.

In Khanbaliq Marco visited the Khan's mint, and what he saw there astonished him, because the Khan's money was not made of gold or silver but of paper. The paper was made from the inner bark of the mulberry tree, whose leaves feed the silkworms, and it was pressed and dried until it was as dark and strong as cloth. Nothing like it had ever been seen in Venice, where merchants still weighed every coin and trusted only the metal inside it.

Workers cut the dark paper into rectangles of different sizes, and each size was worth a different amount, from a few small coins to a large sum. Officials signed every note, and at the end the master of the mint dipped the Khan's seal in red ink and pressed it onto the paper. Only after that did the scrap become money, and Marco calls this process a kind of magic.

Merchants who arrived with gold, pearls or precious stones were paid by the Khan in paper notes, and they took them gladly, for the notes could be spent anywhere in his empire. In this way the ruler gathered an enormous amount of treasure while giving little more than stamped bark in return. Marco jokes that the Khan must have discovered the secret of making gold, since he could turn a pile of bark into a roomful of treasure.

The law of the empire was that every person had to accept the paper notes as if they were gold, and Marco says that anyone who refused might be punished severely. In practice there was little need for force, since the notes were convenient, light and easy to carry on a long journey. Foreign merchants soon learned to expect paper wherever they went, and to spend it before they left the empire.

Notes wore out quickly in the hands of busy people, but the Khan's officials had thought of that, too. Anyone with a torn or dirty note could take it to the mint and swap it for a new one, paying a small percentage as a fee. It was a clever system that kept the paper money fresh and clean, and that also brought in a small but steady income for the state.

In the cold winters of the north, Marco noticed with surprise that the people of Khanbaliq kept their fires going by burning black stones, which were dug from the mountains and carried to the city in carts. Once lit, the stones burned like logs and kept a fire alive through the whole night, which was a great help in a place where firewood was scarce. We call these stones coal, but to a man from Venice, where people burned wood and charcoal, it was something entirely new.

Because the black stones burned so hot and so cheaply, the people of Khanbaliq could keep public baths warm even in the depth of winter. Marco says that they washed several times a week, a custom that struck many Europeans of his time as a luxury and even a danger to health. He himself seems to have enjoyed the baths, and he writes about them with approval.

What impressed Marco most was the Khan's system of messengers, for on every main road stood post houses about twenty-five miles apart, each kept ready with fresh horses. A rider who arrived tired could hand his message to a new rider, or simply change mounts and gallop on towards the next station. Through this network the Khan could learn of trouble in a distant province within a few days.

The royal messengers wore belts hung with little bells, so that the keepers of the next station heard them coming and had a fresh horse ready before they arrived. By changing horses at every post, Marco says, a rider could cover two hundred miles in a single day, and in an emergency even more. No ruler in Europe, and certainly no Venetian merchant, had ever seen a service that could match it for speed or for order.

The Khan had ordered trees to be planted along all the great roads, so that travellers could find shade in summer and see the line of the road when snow covered the ground. He also had large stores of grain built in the towns, and when a harvest failed he sold the grain cheaply or gave it to the poor. Marco was impressed that so powerful a ruler should think of his poorest subjects, and he wrote about it with obvious admiration.

The Khan's birthday, in late September, was celebrated each year with a splendour that Marco could hardly describe. Thousands of lords came to the palace, all of them wearing robes of the same colour, which the Khan himself had given them as a mark of favour. Each robe was decorated with pearls and gold thread, and each lord brought a gift in return.

The greatest festival of the year was the White Feast, held in February at the start of the new year, when the Khan and everyone at his court dressed in white. White, says Marco, was thought to be a lucky colour, and people hoped that it would bring them good fortune for the next twelve months. Even the people in the streets of the capital wore white and greeted one another with gifts.

On the day of the festival, everyone from the richest lords to the humblest officials brought presents to the Khan, and the most prized gifts were white horses. Then came a grand parade of elephants and camels, covered with embroidered cloth and loaded with the Khan's treasures, which marched slowly past the palace gate. Marco says that nothing in Venice could match such a show of power and wealth.

Inside the great hall, the Khan sat at a table on a raised platform, with the empress and his sons beside him, while the other guests were seated in order of rank at long tables below. Everything was arranged so that the ruler could see every face in the room, and every guest could see him. Marco, as a favoured foreigner, was given a seat that was higher than he could have hoped.

The servants who carried the Khan's dishes and cups wore fine silk cloths tied over their mouths and noses, so that their breath could not touch his food. Marco found the custom curious, though he understood that it was a sign of deep respect and of the ruler's high rank. Few kings in Europe, he must have thought, were served with such care, and none was surrounded by quite so much quiet ceremony.

Marco greatly admired the Mongol horsemen, who could ride for ten days at a time without lighting a fire to cook, which meant that they could move far faster than any European army. They lived on mare's milk and on dried milk paste, which they carried in small bags and mixed with water whenever they were hungry. Their toughness had helped to win them the largest empire the world had ever seen.

The Khan kept a great herd of pure white mares, and Marco was told that their milk was drunk only by members of the royal family and a few honoured clans. Each summer, at an ancient ceremony, the Khan poured a little of the milk onto the ground as an offering, in the hope that the spirits would keep his animals safe. It was a reminder that the ruler of China was also a Mongol who had grown up on the grass.

Each spring the Khan left the city for several weeks of hunting, and he was followed by thousands of falconers, huntsmen and attendants with their dogs and trained birds. Marco, who sometimes rode with the party, says that the long lines of riders spread across the plain were a beautiful sight, with the falcons wheeling in the sky above. Many of the animals that were caught were sent back to the palace kitchens.

Because he was old and suffered from gout in his legs, the Khan did not always ride on hunting trips, but travelled instead in a wooden room carried on the backs of four elephants. The room was lined with cloth of gold on the inside and covered with the skins of lions on the outside, and it held a bed on which the Khan could lie. From there he could watch the hunt through the open curtains, and when the hunters sighted game he could send out his falcons from his bed.

On these trips the Khan's camp spread across the plain like a city of tents, with streets of canvas, flags of every colour and thousands of horses grazing round it. His own tent was so big, Marco says, that a thousand knights could stand within it, and its walls were hung with the striped skins of tigers and other beasts. To the young Venetian it must have seemed like a dream from the old romances, only real.

Over the following years the Khan sent Marco on a series of missions to the far provinces of the empire, and he set out each time with a golden tablet and a train of servants. Wherever he went he looked, listened and made notes of prices, crops, customs and curious stories, so that he could report them to the Khan. These journeys, and the notes he made on them, later became the heart of the book that would carry his name across the world.

Marco's road west led him to Taiyuan, a busy city where, he says, grapes grew on the hillsides and wine was made in quantities large enough to supply the whole province. Vineyards were rare in northern China, and a Venetian was pleased to find a familiar drink in such an unfamiliar land. The city also had many workshops where iron was beaten into tools and weapons for the Khan's armies.

A few miles from Khanbaliq the road crossed a river by a magnificent stone bridge, which Marco calls Pulisanghin and describes as having twenty-four arches and marble pillars topped with carved lions. He says that it was about three hundred paces long and wide enough for ten horsemen to ride side by side. The bridge still stands today, and Europeans call it the Marco Polo Bridge in his honour.

From the bridge Marco travelled on to Xi'an, a splendid city famous for its silk and its busy trade, and one of the oldest capitals of China. A son of the Great Khan ruled there from a handsome palace outside the walls, and Marco was received politely as an envoy from his father. The city had been prosperous for centuries, and its streets were crowded with merchants from many lands.

Beyond Xi'an the road climbed into the wild mountains of the south-west, crossing deep valleys where rivers rushed through narrow gorges far below. At last Marco came down into the rich plain of Chengdu, where he admired a long wooden bridge covered by a roof and lined with the stalls of merchants. Such a bridge was more like a street than a road, and he had never seen anything like it.

In the south-west, Marco says, travellers lit fires of green bamboo, which crackled and then burst open with a bang so loud that it could be heard ten miles away. Horses that had not heard the noise before were so frightened that they would break their ropes and run, and the people had to be careful to tie them well. The sound is one of the earliest signs of the firecrackers that Chinese people would later perfect.

Near the border of Tibet, Marco heard about a small deer that produced musk, a strong and costly scent which perfume makers prized all over the world. He also noticed that the people of some villages did not use coins at all, but paid for goods with small cakes of salt stamped with the Khan's seal. In mountains where salt was scarce, this was an eminently sensible kind of money.

In the warm river valleys of Yunnan, Marco saw creatures that he calls great serpents, ten paces long, with two short legs, huge jaws and eyes like loaves of bread. They were, of course, crocodiles, a beast that no European of his day had ever seen alive. The local people hunted them for their skins, and some even ate the meat, which they considered a great delicacy.

In the town that Marco calls Vochan, men and women covered their teeth with thin caps of gold, which they could take off when they ate, and some of them also tattooed their arms and legs with dark patterns. Everyday trade there was done not with coins but with small white cowrie shells, which had to be counted out one by one. Marco, a merchant to his fingertips, took careful note of what each shell was worth.

Marco tells a vivid story of a battle fought around 1277 on the border of Burma, where the king's army had brought hundreds of war elephants with wooden towers on their backs. The Mongol horses were terrified by the huge animals, so the Khan's commander ordered his men to dismount, tie their horses in the trees and shoot arrows at the elephants from cover. Wounded and frightened, the great beasts turned and ran, and the Mongols won the day.

The south of China was still ruled by the Song emperors, and Marco, following Mongol custom, calls the whole region Mangi. It was richer, greener and more crowded than the north, with rice fields, canals and large cities, and Kublai Khan was determined to add it to his empire. The conquest was a long and difficult task that would take years of planning, thousands of soldiers and a great deal of patience.

The great fortress city of Xiangyang stood on a river, protected by high walls, wide water and a loyal and stubborn garrison. The Mongol armies besieged it for about five years, from 1268 to 1273, and could find no way to break in. Its fall was the turning point of the war, since after it the road to the south lay open.

In his book Marco claims that his father and uncle built huge stone-throwing machines that broke the long siege and won the city for the Khan. Historians doubt this, because the siege ended in 1273, two years before the Polos reached the Khan's court, and Chinese records credit two engineers from Persia. It is one of the places where Marco seems to have added himself to a story he heard from others.

To lead the conquest the Khan chose a talented general named Bayan, whom Marco calls Baian Hundred Eyes because, he says, the man noticed everything that happened in his army. The explanation is probably a misunderstanding of a Chinese pun, but it shows how highly the Venetians thought of him. In 1275 Bayan marched down the Yangtze with an enormous army and a fleet of river ships.

Marco was astonished by the Yangtze, which in places stretched so wide that a person standing on one bank could scarcely see the other, and which flowed for thousands of miles through the heart of China. He declares that more ships sailed on this one river than on all the rivers and seas of the Christian world together, and he lists the cities on its banks with growing wonder. It was, he thought, the greatest highway on Earth, and no road in all of Europe could compare with it for traffic.

In 1276 the Song capital Hangzhou, seeing that further resistance was hopeless, opened its gates to Bayan, and the young emperor, who was only a small child, was sent north to the Khan. Marco's account of these events differs from the Chinese records in several details, but all of them agree that the city was spared and not burned. Most of its people carried on with their lives much as before, selling and buying in the markets as the new rulers settled in.

Marco says that the Khan made him governor of the great city of Yangzhou, a post that he held for three years. No Chinese record mentions his name in connection with it, and some historians suspect that he held a smaller office, perhaps in the tax service, and enjoyed describing it in grander terms. Either way, he clearly knew the city and its customs well, and his description of its people and trade is full of convincing detail.

Along the coast near Yangzhou, workers made salt by letting the sea water dry in shallow pools, and then raked it into great white heaps. Marco learned that the Khan collected a heavy tax on every load, and that this single tax brought in an astonishing sum of gold each year. It was one more proof that the Khan's wealth rested on careful and orderly government.

Another wonder that Marco describes is the Grand Canal, a great waterway made by people, which carried rice, silk and other goods from the rich south to the hungry north. Some stretches were many centuries old, and in Marco's time the Khan's engineers were joining them with new channels so that barges could sail all the way to the capital. The scale of the work, he says, was beyond anything that had ever been built in Europe, and he returned to the subject again and again.

At the busy towns along the canal, long lines of barges loaded with rice, salt, silk and timber slid past day and night, and Marco declares that there were so many that nobody could count them. He must sometimes have thought of the crowded waterways of Venice, which suddenly seemed small beside this vast machine of trade. With each mile that Marco travelled along the water, the great cities of the south came closer, and the most splendid of them all was waiting at the end.

Marco came at last to Hangzhou, which he calls Quinsai, a name that he says means the City of Heaven, and he declares it to be the finest and noblest city in the world. Once the capital of the Song emperors, it had passed peacefully into the Khan's hands, and its beauty was almost unharmed. He tells of it at length, and with a joy that no other place in his book receives.

By Marco's reckoning the wall of Hangzhou ran for about a hundred miles, an estimate that seems far too large, though the city really was among the biggest in the world. A great lake lay on one side, and a wide river with many branches ran along the other, so that canals threaded the streets in every direction. It was a place built on water, much as his own native city was, and he felt at home in it at once.

Hangzhou, Marco says, had twelve thousand bridges of stone, which is a figure that modern scholars find very large, though the city undoubtedly had a great many. The arches of the main bridges were so high that a ship could pass beneath them without lowering its mast, which astonished a man who came from the city of the Rialto. Marco, who loved his own city, could scarcely have found a more fitting place to compare with it, and he did so with pride.

The city, Marco explains, had ten great market squares, each of them half a mile across, where on three days a week huge crowds came to buy and sell. The tables were heaped with fish from the lake and the sea, with meat, fruit, vegetables and spices, and the stone warehouses nearby were filled with goods from India and the islands. He declares that the sheer amount of food on sale was astonishing, and that the people of the city bought nearly all of it fresh each day.

Unlike the muddy lanes of most European towns, the streets of Hangzhou were paved with stone and brick, so that people could walk and ride through them in all weathers. Marco says that there were twelve great trades in the city, such as smiths, carpenters and silk workers, each employing a vast number of workshops. A merchant who needed some special skill could find it within a few streets, and could usually find three or four workers who offered it.

Marco noticed with interest that every house in Hangzhou carried a small tablet beside the door, on which were written the names of all the people who lived inside, and even the number of horses they kept. Innkeepers, too, were required to record the name of every guest and the date of his arrival, so that the officials could keep track of the movements of foreigners. A Venetian merchant, whose own city also liked to keep an eye on strangers, would have understood the usefulness of such careful records at once.

On the western side of Hangzhou lay a famous lake, which Marco says was about thirty miles in circuit, though it is in fact much smaller. Its shores were crowded with temples, gardens and the elegant houses of rich families, and willows leaned over the water to touch it. Poets had been praising the lake for centuries, and Marco, having seen it for himself, found that he agreed with every one of them.

On the lake, Marco says, people could hire large pleasure boats with painted cabins, silk awnings and tables set for dinner, and the boatmen would row them gently across the water while the guests feasted. From the middle of the lake, the city looked more beautiful than ever, with its palaces and temples rising from the trees. Nothing in the whole world, Marco declares, was more pleasant than a long summer evening spent on the lake in good company.

Marco visited the old palace of the Song kings, which stood inside a high wall in the heart of the city and which the Khan's governor had been ordered to preserve. It contained many great halls, rooms painted with gold and blue, and gardens with fountains and rare fish, and Marco was told that the last king of the Song had lived there in great luxury. It was a splendid and silent reminder of a vanished court, and Marco walked through its empty halls with a sense of wonder.

At night, Marco says, guards stood watch on every bridge and patrolled the streets, for most of the houses were made of wood and fires broke out often. To protect their goods, rich merchants kept them in stone towers, where the flames could not reach, and in a fire the people carried their belongings there for safety. Order, once again, impressed him as much as wealth did, and he wrote of the city's safety and its gentle people with real respect.

From Hangzhou the road led south through a landscape of green hills, fast rivers and busy market towns, each of which Marco describes in a few brisk lines. After many days he crossed into the province of Fujian, where the mountains were thick with forests and bamboo and the air grew steadily warmer. It was a country that seemed to him richer and more crowded with every mile that the Polos rode, and he never tired of looking.

In the city of Fuzhou, Marco found that ginger and galangal grew in such quantities that they could be bought for a tiny price, and that sugar was made in great amounts. He was told that for a long time people there had boiled the sugar into a rough paste, until some men from Egypt showed them how to refine it with wood ash. It was an early sign of how knowledge travelled along the trade routes, passed from one merchant to another over thousands of miles.

In the small town of Tingiu, which is now called Dehua, Marco saw workshops that made bowls and dishes of a shining white material that we call porcelain. He was told that the clay was piled up and left to age for thirty or forty years before it was used, and that the finished ware was so cheap that three bowls cost less than a Venetian groat. Back in Europe, such pieces would soon be treasured like jewels, and Marco's word for them, porcelain, would enter several languages.

At last Marco reached Zaiton, the port that is now called Quanzhou, which he judged to be one of the two greatest harbours in the whole world. Ships from India and the Spice Islands arrived there all through the year, and the quays were crowded with merchants, porters and customs officers. For a Venetian, it was the perfect place to end an inland journey, since he had grown up among ships and understood a harbour at a glance.

Pepper was the great prize of the spice trade, and Marco claims that for each ship loaded with it that sailed to Alexandria for the Christian world, a hundred came into Zaiton. Whatever the real figure, the port was extremely busy, and the Khan's officers took a large share of every cargo as a tax before the merchants could sell it. The wealth of the harbour helped to pay for the Khan's armies and palaces.

Merchants from India, Persia, Arabia and many other lands lived in or near Zaiton, and the city held temples, mosques and even a few small churches side by side. Marco liked the way so many peoples shared one city and traded peacefully, each in his own language and with his own customs. It was a lesson in tolerance that few towns in Europe could have taught him.

Marco describes the great sea-going ships of China with obvious envy, for they were far bigger and stronger than any vessel that he had seen on the Mediterranean. They were built of fir wood, with two layers of planking, the seams filled with a mixture of lime, hemp and oil, and they carried four masts and many sails. He had no doubt that these were the finest ships on any sea, and he spent many hours examining how they were made.

Inside, the hull of each great ship was divided by strong walls into as many as thirteen watertight compartments, which meant that a leak in one section would flood only that part and not the whole vessel. Even if the ship struck a rock or a whale, Marco says, the crew could repair the damage while the rest of the ship stayed dry. European shipbuilders would not copy the idea for centuries, and Marco was probably the first to describe it to them.

A big ship might carry as many as three hundred sailors, together with merchants, goods and a number of smaller boats that were towed along behind. Marco was amused to find that the crews grew fresh vegetables and ginger in wooden tubs on the deck, so that on long voyages they would not go short of green food. It was a sensible habit that sailors of other nations were slow to adopt.

In the port of Zaiton, Marco heard sailors talk of a rich island far out in the eastern sea, which he calls Cipangu and which we know as Japan. They told him that its king lived in a palace with a roof of pure gold and floors paved with the same metal, a tale that must have thrilled the merchants who heard it. Marco never visited the island, and he is careful to say that he only reports what others told him.

Marco tells how the Khan, tempted by tales of gold, sent two great fleets against Japan, one in 1274 and another in 1281, and how fierce storms wrecked many of the ships. Thousands of soldiers were lost in the waves or left behind on the island, and only a few ever came home to China. The Japanese remembered the storms as a gift of the gods, but to the Khan they were a disaster.

After so many years in China the Polos had grown rich, and they felt a strong wish to see Venice again before they became too old to travel. They also worried that if the aging Khan should die, his enemies might turn against the foreigners who had been his favourites. They needed a way home soon, but they could not leave without his permission.

When Niccolò finally dared to ask for leave to depart, the Khan answered with a firm refusal, saying that he liked the Venetians and would not part with them. He could not understand why men who lived so well in his palace should want to endure the dangers of the road again. The Polos waited and said nothing more, hoping that some chance would one day change his mind and open the road home.

Their chance came when three envoys arrived from Arghun, the Mongol ruler of Persia and a relative of the Great Khan, with a request that was both sad and urgent. Arghun's beloved wife had died, and on her deathbed she had asked that his next wife should be chosen from her own clan. The envoys had come all that way to ask the Khan for a bride.

The Khan chose a girl of seventeen called Kokachin, who belonged to the right family and who, Marco says, was beautiful and wise beyond her years. The envoys met her and were delighted, and they agreed at once to take her home to their king. Nobody seems to have asked what the young woman herself wanted, as was usual in royal marriages of that age.

Fighting between rival Mongol rulers had closed the overland road, so the envoys wanted to take the princess home by sea. Just then Marco returned from a voyage to the coasts of India, and he knew a good deal about the sea route and its dangers. The envoys saw at once that the Venetians, who knew both the Latin lands and the eastern seas, would make ideal guides, and they begged the Khan to let the Polos sail along.

At last the Khan gave way, though it clearly pained him to lose the foreigners he had come to like and trust. He gave the Polos golden tablets that would protect them on their journey, as well as letters addressed to the Pope and to the kings of France, Spain and other Christian lands. It was a mark of the deep respect that he felt for them, and a sign that his heart was heavy at the parting.

The Khan ordered fourteen great ships to be fitted out, each with four masts and many sails, and he loaded them with everything the travellers could need. Marco says that about six hundred people went aboard, not counting the sailors, and that the ships carried supplies enough for two whole years. It was the largest expedition he had ever seen sail from the port of Zaiton.

In about 1291 the fleet left the harbour of Zaiton and set out upon the open sea, with the princess, the three envoys and the three Polos all aboard. Standing on the deck, Marco watched the coast of China slowly sink below the horizon, and he knew that he was unlikely ever to see it again. He had lived there for about seventeen years, and the departure must have been bittersweet.

After some three months at sea, the fleet reached Champa, a hot and green kingdom on the coast of what is now Vietnam. Marco says that its king sent the Khan a yearly gift of elephants, an agreement made after Mongol armies had defeated him in battle some years before. The Polos landed there to rest and to buy fresh supplies for the long road still ahead.

The fleet sailed on past the great island of Java, which the sailors declared to be the richest in the world, with pepper, nutmeg, cloves and other spices growing in abundance. Marco did not land there, and he is careful to say that he is repeating what the sailors told him rather than describing what he saw. The ships then entered the shallow channels near Pentam, where the pilots had to steer with great caution.

At last the fleet reached the north coast of Sumatra, where the monsoon winds were blowing in the wrong direction and no ship could leave. Marco says that they waited for about five months, which was a long time to stay in one place with a princess to look after and a long journey still ahead. Sailors of that age knew that nothing could be done against the wind, so the crews simply waited, mended their ships and told stories.

To keep themselves safe during the long wait, the travellers built a wooden fort with a deep ditch around it, and they bought rice, fish and fruit from the people of the island. Marco tasted wine tapped from the palm tree, and he saw how flour could be made from the soft inside of the sago palm, which struck him as a very odd kind of tree. The weeks passed slowly, but the fort held, the food was plentiful, and the people of the fleet came to no harm during their stay.

On Sumatra, Marco came across a large and heavy animal that he calls a unicorn, because it has a single great black horn in the middle of its forehead. It had feet like an elephant, a thick skin and a taste for lying in mud, and he admits that it was nothing like the graceful white creature of the old tales. We would call it a rhinoceros, and Marco's disappointment is easy to understand when one remembers what he had hoped to see.

In the little kingdom of Perlak, Marco noticed that the townspeople followed the Muslim faith, while the people of the hills kept their own older beliefs. Merchants from Arabia and Persia, who had come there to trade, had taught the town their religion, and Marco saw clearly how faith could travel on the same ships as spices. It was a pattern that was being repeated all along the coasts of the Indian Ocean.

In Ceylon, which is now called Sri Lanka, Marco heard about the island's king, who was said to own the finest ruby in the world, a stone as long as a man's palm and as thick as his arm. The Khan, hearing of it, sent messengers with an offer of a whole city in exchange, but the king answered that he would not sell it for all the treasure on earth. Marco never saw the great ruby himself, but he heard about it from many people.

In Ceylon there is a high and steep mountain that Marco knew as Adam's Peak, and its rock sides were so smooth that pilgrims could climb only with the help of iron chains fixed there long before.
