At the top is a large footprint in the stone, which Muslims said had been left by Adam, the first man, while Buddhists said that it was the print of the Buddha. Marco records both beliefs with respect and without taking sides, and he adds that people of other faiths also climbed the peak to honour it.

Off the southern coast of India, merchants hired divers to bring up oysters from the bottom of a shallow bay, in the hope of finding the pearls that lay inside them. Each diver held his breath for as long as he could, and Marco was told that special men, whom he calls charmers, recited spells to keep the sharks away from the swimmers. The king, he says, took a tenth of all the pearls that were found.

In Mylapore, on the south-eastern coast of India, Marco visited a small church where, according to local tradition, the Apostle Thomas had been laid to rest after his death. Christians and many local people alike came to the shrine as pilgrims, and some of them carried away a little red earth from the spot, which they believed could cure illness. Marco, who was a devout Christian, wrote about the place with great respect, and he was glad to find his own faith so far from home.

Along the Malabar coast of India, Marco saw gardens of pepper, ginger and cinnamon, and a steady stream of ships arriving from Arabia and from the east with cargoes of horses, copper and silk. He also heard that pirates worked those waters in large fleets, spreading out across the sea in lines so that no merchant ship could easily slip past them. The Polos, with a princess and hundreds of passengers aboard, must have sailed those waters with their eyes wide open and their weapons close at hand.

After about two years at sea, the ships came at last to Hormuz, but the voyage had cost the expedition dearly. Marco says that of the six hundred passengers who had boarded in Zaiton, only eighteen were still alive, and that two of the three envoys had died as well. The Polos and the princess were among those who survived, which must have felt like a small miracle.

On arriving, the travellers learned that King Arghun had died while they were still at sea, and that his brother Gaikhatu was ruling the country after the death of his brother. The Polos asked him what ought to be done with the princess, who now had no husband, and with the letters that they were carrying from the Khan. It was an awkward situation for everyone concerned, and nobody in the Persian court wanted to be the one who made the wrong choice.

Gaikhatu decided that the princess should marry Arghun's son, Ghazan, who was a young man of about twenty-two and was then guarding the northern borders. The marriage took place, and Marco says that when the time came to part with the Polos, who had looked after her for two long years, the princess wept bitterly. Kokachin had come a very long way, and she had no family in the whole of Persia.

The Polos rested for several months in Tabriz, the rich Persian city that they already knew from their journey east, and they sold part of their goods there. Before they left, Gaikhatu gave them golden tablets like those of the Great Khan, which would let them travel safely through his lands and find fresh horses and food on the way. They were nearly home, at least by their own standards, and the road from Tabriz to the sea was one that they now knew well.

From Tabriz the Polos rode north-west across the mountains to Trebizond, a busy port on the south-eastern shore of the Black Sea, where they found merchant ships bound for the west. It was a joy to see Greek and Italian sailors again, and to hear voices speaking languages that Marco had not heard in many years. They paid for their passage with some of the gold they had earned in China, and they sailed towards Constantinople on the first fair wind.

The Polos crossed the Black Sea and arrived in Constantinople, the great city where Niccolò and Maffeo had first prospered more than thirty years earlier and where the three of them paused to rest. From there they took ship through the Greek islands towards the Adriatic Sea, passing familiar harbours one after another. Every mile now brought them closer to the lagoon where it had all begun.

In 1295, after an absence of some twenty-four years, the three Polos finally sailed into the lagoon of Venice, tired, sunburnt and dressed in coarse Mongol clothes that had seen a great deal of weather. Marco had left as a teenager and came back a man of about forty, and his father and uncle were now old men with lined faces and foreign ways. The city they remembered had changed as well, and they walked its narrow streets like visitors in a place they had once known by heart.

At the family house, the relatives stared at the three weathered strangers on the doorstep and could hardly believe that they were the long-lost Polos, who had been given up for dead. The men had a foreign look about them, and they spoke their native Venetian with an odd, hesitant accent, as if they had half forgotten the words. It took a good deal of time and many questions about old family secrets before anyone was willing to believe that these were the men they had mourned.

A famous later story says that the Polos held a feast and then cut open their old, worn coats, from which rubies, emeralds and other jewels poured onto the table. An editor named Ramusio first wrote the tale down more than two hundred years later, and it may well have been invented. Yet it is a good picture of how the Polos came home, with their wealth hidden in plain sight.

Soon the people of Venice began to call Marco Il Milione, a nickname that means The Million, and a small courtyard near the family house, the Corte del Milion, still keeps the name today. Nobody is quite sure how he earned it, but scholars have suggested that it came from his wealth, from the huge numbers in his stories or simply from a family name. Whatever its meaning, the name stuck to him and to his book for centuries.

Venice and Genoa were the two great sea powers of Italy, and for generations they had competed for the trade of the eastern Mediterranean and the Black Sea. In the 1290s that rivalry turned once more into open war, and Venice called on its wealthy citizens to supply ships and men. Marco Polo, who was now a rich man, may well have been among those who answered the call.

According to an old tradition, Marco paid for a war galley out of his own money and sailed with the Venetian fleet as one of its commanders. The records of the time are not clear on this point, and some historians are doubtful, but it is certain that he was captured in the war. A merchant who had crossed the whole of Asia could surely also manage a ship, and Venice needed every capable man it could find.

In September 1298 the two fleets met off the island of Curzola, in the Adriatic Sea, and after a long and bitter fight the Genoese, led by the admiral Lamba Doria, won a great victory. Many Venetian ships were captured or lost, and thousands of Venetian sailors and soldiers were taken prisoner and carried away to Genoa. Among them, according to the tradition, was Marco Polo, who had survived the deserts of Asia but could not escape the war galleys of a rival city.

Marco was carried to Genoa with the other prisoners and held there while the two cities slowly argued over the terms on which the war could end. It was an uncomfortable and uncertain time, since nobody knew how long the negotiations would last, and some prisoners remained locked up for years. Marco, who had survived the deserts of Asia, now faced a very different kind of waiting.

In the prison Marco met a fellow captive named Rustichello of Pisa, who had been in Genoese hands since the sea battle of Meloria fourteen years before. Rustichello was a professional writer of romances, which were the popular adventure stories of the age, filled with knights, ladies and the legendary King Arthur. He listened with growing fascination to the tales that Marco had to tell, and he soon saw that they would make a remarkable book.

Day after day Marco described the lands he had seen, while Rustichello, with a quill and sheets of paper, wrote down every word as fast as he could. Tradition says that Marco sent to Venice for his notebooks, which helped him recall the names of cities, the distances between them and the prices of goods. The result was a book that was full of facts, figures and surprising stories, quite unlike any romance that Rustichello had ever written.

The book was written in French, which was the language of romance and travel stories across much of Europe, and it opens in the grand style that Rustichello loved. Its first words call upon emperors, kings, dukes, knights and all other people who wish to learn about the different races and kingdoms of the world to read the book and find out. The tone was Rustichello's, but the facts and the wonders came from Marco, and the two voices together made something quite new.

The book's pages move from city to city and from country to country, describing roads, markets, religions, foods, animals and the habits of the people who lived in each place. Marco usually says plainly whether he saw a thing himself or only heard about it from someone else, which gives the book an honesty that modern readers appreciate. Its title was the Description of the World, though most people simply call it the Travels, and in Italy it is still known as Il Milione.

In 1299 Genoa and Venice finally agreed on peace, and the Venetian prisoners were set free and allowed to go home. Marco returned to Venice, where he would spend the rest of his life, and the book that he and Rustichello had made together in the prison soon began to be copied. There is no record that the two men ever met again, though their names were joined for ever on the first page of the book.

Back in Venice, Marco married Donata Badoer, the daughter of a merchant, and the couple had three daughters, whose names were Fantina, Bellela and Moreta. He lived as a respected merchant in a house near the church of San Giovanni Crisostomo, and he seems to have been content with an ordinary life after so many years of extraordinary travel. The great adventurer had become a family man, and his days were now filled with accounts, letters and the small noises of a busy house.

In those years nobody in Europe had yet invented printing, so the book spread slowly, as scribes copied it out by hand, and every copy differed a little from the one before. Within a few years it had been translated from French into Latin, Italian and other languages, and about a hundred and fifty of these early manuscripts still survive. No other travel book of the age was copied so often, and few books of any kind travelled so far from their author's home.

Some readers believed every word in the book, while others, who had never travelled beyond their own valleys, felt sure that Marco was inventing marvels to amuse them. The huge numbers that he quoted for cities, bridges and ships made the doubters smile, and some may have used the nickname Il Milione in a mocking way. Still, even the doubters wanted a copy to read, and they argued about it in every town where it arrived.

Modern critics have pointed out that Marco never mentions tea, chopsticks, the printing of books or the Great Wall. They find it hard to believe that a man who lived in China for seventeen years would leave them all out, and Chinese records, too, do not name him. The questions are fair ones, and historians have been debating them for many years without reaching complete agreement.

Defenders reply that the famous stone Great Wall was built long after Marco's day, and that Persian was a common language at the Mongol court, which explains his Persian place names. His descriptions of paper money, coal, salt taxes and the post system are accurate as well. Most historians today think that Marco did go to China, and his book is a priceless source, even though a few of its stories come from other people.

In January 1324, when Marco was about seventy years old and clearly ill, he made a will in Venice, which still survives in the city's archives. He left money to his wife and his three daughters and to local churches, and he freed a servant named Peter, a Tartar, who had probably come with him from the East. Soon afterwards he died, and he was buried in the church of San Lorenzo.

A famous story, which may or may not be true, says that on his deathbed Marco's friends urged him to confess that the book was exaggerated and to take back its wildest tales. He is said to have answered that he had not told even half of what he had really seen. Whether he said it or not, it fits the man very well, for he had indeed seen far more than any book could hold.

In the 1450s a Venetian monk named Fra Mauro drew an enormous round map of the world, in which Asia was shown in far greater detail than any earlier European map had managed. He took many of its names, from Cathay and Cipangu to Quinsai and Zaiton, straight from Marco's book, and some of them were still there on maps three hundred years later. A merchant's memories, written down in a prison cell, had become a lasting part of the geography of the world.

Christopher Columbus owned a printed copy of Marco's book and wrote many notes in its margins, marking the passages about gold, spices and the rich island of Cipangu. In 1492 he sailed west across the Atlantic in the hope of reaching the lands of the Great Khan, and he was astonished to find a continent that neither Marco nor anyone in Europe had known. He never understood how far he really was from Asia, and he died still believing that he had found its eastern edge.

Over the next centuries many travellers made their way east with Marco's book in their bags, and slowly the places that he had described were found again. Around 1600, Jesuit missionaries such as Matteo Ricci, along with a traveller named Benedict Goës, showed at last that Cathay, the land of the Great Khan, was the same country as the China that Europeans already knew. The old Venetian's report, which so many people had laughed at for three hundred years, had been right about the main facts all along.

Today the Travels of Marco Polo is read in dozens of languages across the world, and the airport of Venice carries the name of the boy who set out from its lagoon in 1271. Historians still argue over some of his claims, but few doubt that the book opened Europe's eyes to a larger world of cities, ships, markets and kindly strangers. It remains one of the great invitations to curiosity, and anyone who opens it will be walking Marco's road.
